These activation deltas are derived from reference completions that combine the ground-truth answer with a model-generated explanation to facilitate semantically enriched, example-specific steering. The injection weights are optimized per prompt using Optuna, targeting a joint objective that balances token overlap (factual alignment) and perplexity (fluency proxy). Evaluation employs a composite score integrating token overlap and LLM-graded quality, encompassing factual accuracy, coherence, and relevance. Empirical results on 260 SimpleQA prompts (selected from 500 where the baseline failed) showcase the efficacy of segmented steering. Using Gemma-2-2B-IT with 8-bit quantization, segmented steering achieves an accuracy of 25.4% (outputs scoring $\geq 0.6$), outperforming the baseline at 3.5% and full-layer steering at 16.2%. Under the stricter SimpleQA rubric, segmented steering boosts fully correct responses from 0.0% to 13.1%. These findings highlight the strengths of segmented, dynamic intervention strategies and the promise of per-prompt, full-network activation control. Fusion Steering is also amenable to sparse representations, such as Neuronpedia or sparse crosscoders, suggesting a promising direction for interpretable and scalable activation-level control in LLMs.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Steering Effectiveness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can the reliability of activation-based steering in LLMs be diagnosed using internal model signals such as entropy and KL divergence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that internal mechanistic signals (NBF and KL divergence) can predict steering effectiveness and introduces rotation-based steering as a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods.
papers.conclusion: Internal mechanistic signals can predict steering effectiveness, and rotation-based steering provides a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods, making steering a more measurable and predictable process.
papers.key_findings:
LLM judges (ChatGPT-4o-mini and Gemini-Flash-2.5) show substantial agreement in evaluating steering outputs after correcting for calibration bias.
Effective steering is characterized by structured entropy preservation (NBF) and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps.
Internal signals (NBF, KL, attention patterns) can predict steering quality with reasonable accuracy.
Rotation-based steering outperforms naive additive steering in terms of steering-coherence trade-off.
Attention patterns show a drop in confidence immediately after the intervention layer, correlating with coherence.
papers.limitation:
Limited conceptual coverage (only nine target concepts).
Focus on GEMMA model family, may not generalize to newer models.
Regression formulation requires further refinement.
Label noise from LLM-based judges and qualitative nature of tasks.
papers.abstract: Activation-based steering enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to exhibit targeted behaviors by intervening on intermediate activations without retraining. Despite its widespread use, the mechanistic factors that govern when steering succeeds or fails remain poorly understood, as prior work has relied primarily on black-box outputs or LLM-based judges. In this study, we investigate whether the reliability of steering can be diagnosed using internal model signals. We focus on two information-theoretic measures: the entropy-derived Normalized Branching Factor (NBF), and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between steered activations and targeted concepts in the vocabulary space. We hypothesize that effective steering corresponds to structured entropy preservation and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps. Building on a reliability study demonstrating high inter-judge agreement between two architecturally distinct LLMs, we use LLM-generated annotations as ground truth and show that these mechanistic signals provide meaningful predictive power for identifying successful steering and estimating failure probability. We further introduce a stronger evaluation baseline for Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-based steering, the two most widely adopted activation-steering methods.

papers.title: Cross-model Transferability among Large Language Models on the Platonic Representations of Concepts
papers.research_question: How can conceptual representations (steering vectors) be transferred across different large language models to enable cross-model behavioral control?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L-Cross Modulation, a linear transformation method to transfer steering vectors across LLMs, demonstrating that conceptual representations are linearly alignable and transferable, even from weaker to stronger models.
papers.conclusion: Cross-model transferability of conceptual representations is achievable via linear transformations, revealing a fundamental universality in how LLMs encode concepts, paving the way for more universal and adaptable language models.
papers.key_findings:
L-Cross Modulation effectively modulates target LLMs using steering vectors transferred from source LLMs.
The linear transformation matrix generalizes across different concepts, enabling alignment of SVs for multiple concepts.
Weak-to-strong transferability: SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively modulate the behavior of larger LLMs.
papers.limitation:
The scope of concepts is limited to eleven benchmark concepts; creating more datasets is resource-intensive.
The evaluation metrics are diverse and may not generalize fully to all concepts.
The hyper-parameter (β) for applying steering vectors is manually tuned rather than automatically optimized.
future_direction: Expand to more high-level concepts with additional datasets.
Develop a unified, comprehensive evaluation framework including a standardized dataset and benchmark.
Automatically determine optimal hyperparameters for applying steering vectors.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical research frontier. Prior research has shown that a single LLM's concept representations can be captured as steering vectors (SVs), enabling the control of LLM behavior (e.g., towards generating harmful content). Our work takes a novel approach by exploring the intricate relationships between concept representations across different LLMs, drawing an intriguing parallel to Plato's Allegory of the Cave. In particular, we introduce a linear transformation method to bridge these representations and present three key findings: 1) Concept representations across different LLMs can be effectively aligned using simple linear transformations, enabling efficient cross-model transfer and behavioral control via SVs. 2) This linear transformation generalizes across concepts, facilitating alignment and control of SVs representing different concepts across LLMs. 3) A weak-to-strong transferability exists between LLM concept representations, whereby SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively control the behavior of larger LLMs.

papers.title: Prototype-Based Dynamic Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we amplify large language model reasoning in an adaptive, instruction-free manner without fine-tuning or prompt engineering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Prototype-Based Dynamic Steering (PDS), a test-time method that amplifies LLM reasoning by constructing input-specific steering vectors via projection onto learned reasoning prototypes, without fine-tuning or prompt engineering.
papers.conclusion: PDS is an effective inference-time method for enhancing LLM reasoning by leveraging prototype-based dynamic steering, revealing latent reasoning structure and outperforming static steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
PDS consistently improves accuracy across GSM8K, AQuA-RAT, and BIG-Bench tasks without fine-tuning or prompt engineering.
PDS outperforms the static difference-of-means steering method.
PDS improves reasoning even when explicit step-by-step instructions are omitted (Anti-CoT setting), indicating it strengthens latent reasoning processes.
PDS preserves output format in Anti-CoT setting while still improving accuracy.
The improvements are achieved through directional guidance rather than magnitude scaling, as normalized prototypes yield similar performance.
papers.limitation:
Prototype discovery relies on a predefined dataset of reasoning traces and may not generalize optimally to domains with different reasoning styles.
Effectiveness is not uniform across all tasks; improvements are more modest when the model's baseline reasoning capability is already near saturation.
Tasks that rely more heavily on domain-specific knowledge rather than on compositional or step-by-step reasoning offer fewer opportunities for PDS to induce substantial gains.
Steering techniques can be misused to create jailbreak cases or amplify undesited behaviors.
future_direction: Extend prototype discovery techniques
Apply dynamic steering cross-modally
papers.abstract: Despite impressive breadth, LLMs still rely on explicit reasoning instructions or static, one-fits-all steering methods, leaving a gap for adaptive, instruction-free reasoning amplification. We present Prototype-Based Dynamic Steering (PDS), a test-time method that amplifies large language model (LLM) reasoning without adding or altering instructions. We introduce "reasoning prototypes" by clustering activation differences between Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and neutral prompts. At inference, an input's hidden state is projected onto these prototypes to form an instance-specific steering vector. Evaluated on GSM8K, AQuA-RAT, and BIG-Bench tasks, PDS consistently improves accuracy without fine-tuning or prompt engineering. Notably, the gains persist even when CoT is explicitly suppressed to improve cost-efficiency, indicating that the intervention strengthens latent reasoning processes rather than inducing a superficial behavioral shift. These results position dynamic, prototype-guided steering as a lightweight alternative to training-time approaches for enhancing LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Identifying Cooperative Personalities in Multi-agent Contexts through Personality Steering with Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How do personality traits, steered via representation engineering, affect LLM behavior and cooperation in multi-agent games like the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma?
papers.core_contribution: Personality steering using representation engineering effectively promotes cooperation in LLM-based multi-agent systems, but with a trade-off between cooperation and vulnerability to exploitation.
papers.conclusion: Personality steering through representation engineering effectively promotes cooperation in LLM-based multi-agent systems, providing a foundation for future work in cooperative AI agents.
papers.key_findings:
Steering towards agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness reduces troublemaking rates to zero.
High agreeableness increases exploitability, highlighting a trade-off between cooperation and vulnerability.
Agreeableness and conscientiousness lower lying rates, promoting honesty regardless of opponent behavior.
Models steered towards agreeableness and conscientiousness achieve better collective outcomes but worse individual outcomes.
Personality-steered behavior aligns with human psychological traits in similar contexts.
papers.limitation:
Limited to Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma variants and a single payoff matrix.
Effectiveness across different LLM architectures and tasks remains an open question.
Real-world multi-agent interactions involve more complex incentives.
future_direction: Explore diverse game-theoretic frameworks beyond IPD
Validate results across broader contexts and applications
Investigate effectiveness across different LLM architectures
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain autonomous capabilities, their coordination in multi-agent settings becomes increasingly important. However, they often struggle with cooperation, leading to suboptimal outcomes. Inspired by Axelrod's Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD) tournaments, we explore how personality traits influence LLM cooperation. Using representation engineering, we steer Big Five traits (e.g., Agreeableness, Conscientiousness) in LLMs and analyze their impact on IPD decision-making. Our results show that higher Agreeableness and Conscientiousness improve cooperation but increase susceptibility to exploitation, highlighting both the potential and limitations of personality-based steering for aligning AI agents.

papers.title: Multi-Attribute Steering of Language Models via Targeted Intervention
papers.research_question: How to scale inference-time intervention to multi-attribute settings with conflicts, such as enhancing helpfulness while reducing toxicity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MAT-STEER, a framework for multi-attribute steering via token-level intervention with gating and alignment objectives, outperforming existing methods on QA and generation tasks.
papers.conclusion: MAT-STEER effectively steers LLMs for multiple conflicting attributes through token-level interventions, demonstrating improved accuracy, alignment, and generalization with less data.
papers.key_findings:
MAT-STEER achieves higher accuracy on QA tasks like TruthfulQA, Toxigen, and BBQ compared to baselines.
On generation tasks, MAT-STEER has higher win rates for attributes like helpfulness, correctness, and coherence.
MAT-STEER is data-efficient, requiring less than 20% of training data to match fine-tuning performance.
The method generalizes to other tasks such as FaithEval and HH-RLHF without degrading original capabilities.
Ablation studies show that each component of MAT-STEER contributes to its performance.
papers.limitation:
May struggle with highly complex or unsteerable attributes.
Relies on a small set of data for creating steering vectors.
future_direction: Expanding the approach to a wider array of tasks.
papers.abstract: Inference-time intervention (ITI) has emerged as a promising method for steering large language model (LLM) behavior in a particular direction (e.g., improving helpfulness) by intervening on token representations without costly updates to the LLM's parameters. However, existing ITI approaches fail to scale to multi-attribute settings with conflicts, such as enhancing helpfulness while also reducing toxicity. To address this, we introduce Multi-Attribute Targeted Steering (MAT-Steer), a novel steering framework designed for selective token-level intervention across multiple attributes. MAT-Steer learns steering vectors using an alignment objective that shifts the model's internal representations of undesirable outputs closer to those of desirable ones while enforcing sparsity and orthogonality among vectors for different attributes, thereby reducing inter-attribute conflicts. We evaluate MAT-Steer in two distinct settings: (i) on question answering (QA) tasks where we balance attributes like truthfulness, bias, and toxicity; (ii) on generative tasks where we simultaneously improve attributes like helpfulness, correctness, and coherence. MAT-Steer outperforms existing ITI and parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches across both task types (e.g., 3% average accuracy gain across QA tasks and 55.82% win rate against the best ITI baseline).

papers.title: Comparing Bottom-Up and Top-Down Steering Approaches on In-Context Learning Tasks
papers.research_question: What is the comparative effectiveness of bottom-up (function vectors) and top-down (in-context vectors) steering approaches on diverse in-context learning tasks, and under what conditions does each method excel?
papers.core_contribution: Bottom-up function vectors excel at precise functional tasks but struggle with behavioral shifts, while top-down in-context vectors are effective for behavioral shifts but less reliable for precise tasks, highlighting complementary strengths and limitations of the two steering approaches.
papers.conclusion: Both bottom-up and top-down steering methods are effective only on specific types of in-context learning tasks and cannot fully replace in-context learning, highlighting the need for a unified evaluation benchmark and better understanding of in-context learning mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Function vectors (FVs) outperform in-context vectors (ICVs) on all functional tasks (antonym, capitalize, country-capital, synonym) across zero-shot, few-shot, and natural text settings.
In-context vectors (ICVs) outperform function vectors (FVs) on behavioral tasks (detoxification, sentiment transfer), but with high variance and sensitivity to demonstration data.
ICVs are prone to causing fluency degradation and are less robust when applied in different contexts, while FVs generalize better to out-of-distribution settings.
FV performance is strongly correlated with the causal indirect effect (CIE) of attention heads, indicating that FVs rely on the existence of attention heads that significantly affect task performance.
Both steering methods have significant limitations and cannot serve as a general substitute for in-context learning, emphasizing the need for a unified evaluation benchmark.
papers.limitation:
The study only compares FVs and ICVs on a relatively small set of functional and behavioral tasks, so results may not generalize to an expanded set of tasks.
The work only considers two steering methods, so findings may not generalize to all bottom-up or top-down approaches for vector steering or interpretability.
future_direction: Expanding the scope of the study to other tasks, models, and steering methods.
Developing explanations for the variable performance of FVs and ICVs to improve understanding of in-context learning in LLMs.
papers.abstract: A key objective of interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) is to develop methods for robustly steering models toward desired behaviors. To this end, two distinct approaches to interpretability -- ``bottom-up" and ``top-down" -- have been presented, but there has been little quantitative comparison between them. We present a case study comparing the effectiveness of representative vector steering methods from each branch: function vectors (FV; arXiv:2310.15213), as a bottom-up method, and in-context vectors (ICV; arXiv:2311.06668) as a top-down method. While both aim to capture compact representations of broad in-context learning tasks, we find they are effective only on specific types of tasks: ICVs outperform FVs in behavioral shifting, whereas FVs excel in tasks requiring more precision. We discuss the implications for future evaluations of steering methods and for further research into top-down and bottom-up steering given these findings.

papers.title: MSRS: Adaptive Multi-Subspace Representation Steering for Attribute Alignment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to jointly steer multiple attributes in Large Language Models without interference and undesirable trade-offs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MSRS, a framework for multi-attribute steering that reduces interference by allocating orthogonal subspaces for each attribute and a shared subspace with dynamic weighting.
papers.conclusion: MSRS provides an effective and scalable solution for multi-attribute steering in LLMs, balancing attribute control while preserving model utility.
papers.key_findings:
MSRS significantly reduces attribute conflicts and outperforms existing steering methods across multiple attributes and models.
MSRS generalizes effectively to diverse downstream tasks, improving performance on benchmarks like HellaSwag and GLUE.
The dynamic token-level steering mechanism identifies and intervenes on semantically relevant tokens, enabling fine-grained control.
papers.abstract: Activation steering offers a promising approach to controlling the behavior of Large Language Models by directly manipulating their internal activations. However, most existing methods struggle to jointly steer multiple attributes, often resulting in interference and undesirable trade-offs. To address this challenge, we propose Multi-Subspace Representation Steering (MSRS), a novel framework for effective multi-attribute steering via subspace representation fine-tuning. MSRS reduces inter-attribute interference by allocating orthogonal subspaces to each attribute, isolating their influence within the model's representation space. MSRS also incorporates a hybrid subspace composition strategy: it combines attribute-specific subspaces for unique steering directions with a shared subspace for common steering directions. A dynamic weighting function learns to efficiently integrate these components for precise control. During inference, MSRS introduces a token-level steering mechanism that dynamically identifies and intervenes on the most semantically relevant tokens, enabling fine-grained behavioral modulation. Experimental results show that MSRS significantly reduces attribute conflicts, surpasses existing methods across a range of attributes, and generalizes effectively to diverse downstream tasks.

papers.title: On the Non-Identifiability of Steering Vectors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether steering vectors in large language models are identifiable from input-output behavior, given the null space of the Jacobian.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that steering vectors in large language models are non-identifiable due to the null space of the Jacobian, meaning infinitely many geometrically distinct vectors produce equivalent behavioral effects.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors are fundamentally non-identifiable, implying that behavioral equivalence is insufficient for interpretability claims and structural constraints are needed for reliable alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors are non-identifiable under white-box single-layer access due to null-space ambiguity.
Orthogonal perturbations to steering vectors achieve near-equivalent efficacy with negligible effect sizes.
Vectors extracted by different methods (contrastive mean and PCA) are geometrically distinct but behaviorally equivalent.
Non-identifiability persists across diverse prompt distributions and throughout the operational steering range.
The null space is high-dimensional, with most activation directions being semantically inert.
papers.limitation:
Empirical validation covers only two models at mid-network layers across five semantic traits.
Does not test whether structural interventions such as independence constraints can recover identifiable representations.
Does not formally verify that the semantic null-space coincides with the Jacobian null-space.
future_direction: Testing explicit structural interventions for recovering identifiable representations.
Extending the analysis to the exact nonlinear regime beyond linear approximation.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods are widely used to control large language model (LLM) behavior and are often interpreted as revealing meaningful internal representations. This interpretation assumes steering directions are identifiable and uniquely recoverable from input-output behavior. We show that, under white-box single-layer access, steering vectors are fundamentally non-identifiable due to large equivalence classes of behaviorally indistinguishable interventions. Empirically, we show that orthogonal perturbations achieve near-equivalent efficacy with negligible effect sizes across multiple models and traits. Critically, we show that the non-identifiability is a robust geometric property that persists across diverse prompt distributions. These findings reveal fundamental interpretability limits and highlight the need for structural constraints beyond behavioral testing to enable reliable alignment interventions.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Steering Strength
papers.research_question: How does the steering strength α control the trade-off between steering efficacy and distortion in next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a theoretical analysis of steering strength in LLMs, characterizing its effect on next-token probabilities, concept probability, and cross-entropy, and validates the predictions empirically.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework accurately predicts the empirical behavior of steering strength, providing guidelines for choosing α to balance steering efficacy and output quality.
papers.key_findings:
Next-token probability increases exhibit a bump behavior for most tokens, with off-target tokens peaking earlier than target tokens.
Target concept probability increases sigmoidally with steering strength.
Cross-entropy degrades quadratically with steering strength near zero.
The large-α limit of steered logits converges to a fixed direction determined by the steering vector.
Steering strength α should be chosen adaptively per prompt for optimal effect.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical model assumes a simplified dataset where concepts correspond to disjoint vocabulary subsets, which is unrealistic.
The analysis assumes perfect training of the model, which may not hold in practice.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex datasets and models.
Adaptive choice of steering strength α per input prompt.
papers.abstract: A popular approach to post-training control of large language models (LLMs) is the steering of intermediate latent representations. Namely, identify a well-chosen direction depending on the task at hand and perturbs representations along this direction at inference time. While many propositions exist to pick this direction, considerably less is understood about how to choose the magnitude of the move, whereas its importance is clear: too little and the intended behavior does not emerge, too much and the model's performance degrades beyond repair. In this work, we propose the first theoretical analysis of steering strength. We characterize its effect on next token probability, presence of a concept, and cross-entropy, deriving precise qualitative laws governing these quantities. Our analysis reveals surprising behaviors, including non-monotonic effects of steering strength. We validate our theoretical predictions empirically on eleven language models, ranging from a small GPT architecture to modern models.

papers.title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do various representation-based steering methods compare to prompting and finetuning in terms of concept detection and model steering for language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AXBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating steering and concept detection methods, and finds that prompting outperforms representation-based methods for steering, while difference-in-means and probes are best for detection, with the novel ReFT-r1 method being competitive on both tasks.
papers.conclusion: Representation steering methods largely lag behind prompting and finetuning, but ReFT-r1 shows that steering can be improved with comprehensive benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting is the best method for model steering, outperforming all representation-based methods.
Difference-in-means, linear probes, and ReFT-r1 perform best for concept detection with no significant difference between them.
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are not competitive compared to other methods on both steering and detection.
ReFT-r1, a novel weakly-supervised method, is competitive on both steering and detection tasks while offering interpretability advantages.
The AXBENCH benchmark enables comprehensive evaluation and comparison of steering methods.
papers.limitation: Hyperparameter tuning might underestimate steering performance due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Extend AXBENCH to arbitrary concept descriptions and add new evaluation tasks as better feature-labelling techniques and steering approaches emerge.
papers.abstract: Fine-grained steering of language model outputs is essential for safety and reliability. Prompting and finetuning are widely used to achieve these goals, but interpretability researchers have proposed a variety of representation-based techniques as well, including sparse autoencoders (SAEs), linear artificial tomography, supervised steering vectors, linear probes, and representation finetuning. At present, there is no benchmark for making direct comparisons between these proposals. Therefore, we introduce AxBench, a large-scale benchmark for steering and concept detection, and report experiments on Gemma-2-2B and 9B. For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive. We introduce a novel weakly-supervised representational method (Rank-1 Representation Finetuning; ReFT-r1), which is competitive on both tasks while providing the interpretability advantages that prompting lacks. Along with AxBench, we train and publicly release SAE-scale feature dictionaries for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean.

papers.title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Whether in-context learning and activation steering are instances of a broader framework for controlling LLM behavior, and how they jointly affect model behavior.
papers.core_contribution: Presents a Bayesian belief dynamics model that unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior under both interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Bayesian belief dynamics model unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior and revealing a phase boundary between interventions.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning and activation steering jointly affect behavior, creating a phase boundary modulated by context and activations.
The Bayesian model predicts sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates and additivity of interventions in log-belief space.
The model predicts crossover points (N*) where behavior transitions between concepts, with high correlation to empirical data.
The linear representation hypothesis holds within a range of steering magnitudes, beyond which behavior breaks down.
The model generalizes across different LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and datasets (persona, sentiment).
papers.limitation: The linear representation hypothesis breaks down with large steering magnitudes, leading to chance behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be controlled at inference time through prompts (in-context learning) and internal activations (activation steering). Different accounts have been proposed to explain these methods, yet their common goal of controlling model behavior raises the question of whether these seemingly disparate methodologies can be seen as specific instances of a broader framework. Motivated by this, we develop a unifying, predictive account of LLM control from a Bayesian perspective. Specifically, we posit that both context- and activation-based interventions impact model behavior by altering its belief in latent concepts: steering operates by changing concept priors, while in-context learning leads to an accumulation of evidence. This results in a closed-form Bayesian model that is highly predictive of LLM behavior across context- and activation-based interventions in a set of domains inspired by prior work on many-shot in-context learning. This model helps us explain prior empirical phenomena - e.g., sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates - while predicting novel ones - e.g., additivity of both interventions in log-belief space, which results in distinct phases such that sudden and dramatic behavioral shifts can be induced by slightly changing intervention controls. Taken together, this work offers a unified account of prompt-based and activation-based control of LLM behavior, and a methodology for empirically predicting the effects of these interventions.

papers.title: Language Steering for Multilingual In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does language identity occupy structured directions in activation space, and can a simple activation offset improve multilingual in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces language vectors, a training-free method that improves multilingual in-context learning by steering activations, and shows that language identity occupies structured directions in activation space.
papers.conclusion: Language vectors improve multilingual in-context learning and encode meaningful linguistic structure, supporting the hypothesis that language identity occupies structured directions in activation space.
papers.key_findings:
Language vectors improve performance over baselines across tasks and languages.
Vectors encode linguistic structure, with related languages clustering together.
Vectors transfer across tasks, indicating they capture language-specific rather than task-specific information.
Steering is most effective in early to middle layers.
The method is training-free and requires no parameter updates.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters are selected per language via validation performance, which requires held-out data and may not generalize to new languages or domains.
Evaluation is limited to instruction-tuned decoder-only models.
Certain task transfers fail (e.g., MSVAMP to XNLI).
future_direction: Extending the approach to languages without parallel data.
Applying language vectors to generative tasks such as summarization.
Predicting steering effectiveness without exhaustive hyperparameter search.
papers.abstract: While multilingual large language models have gained widespread adoption, their performance on non-English languages remains substantially inferior to English. This disparity is particularly evident in in-context learning scenarios, where providing demonstrations in English but testing on non-English inputs leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we hypothesize that LLMs develop a universal semantic space for understanding languages, where different languages are encoded as distinct directions within this space. Based on this hypothesis, we propose language vectors -- a training-free language steering approach that leverages activation differences between source and target languages to guide model behavior. We steer the model generations by adding the vector to the intermediate model activations during inference. This is done to make the model's internal representations shift towards the target language space without any parameter updates. We evaluate our method across three datasets and test on a total of 19 languages on three different models. Our results show consistent improvements on multilingual in-context learning over baselines across all tasks and languages tested. Beyond performance gains, hierarchical clustering of steering vectors reveals meaningful linguistic structure aligned with language families. These vectors also successfully transfer across tasks, demonstrating that these representations are task-agnostic.

papers.title: SAE-SSV: Supervised Steering in Sparse Representation Spaces for Reliable Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control large language model behavior in open-ended generation settings by using supervised steering in sparse, interpretable representation spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a supervised steering framework (SAE-SSV) that constrains interventions to a sparse, task-relevant latent subspace identified via labeled data and sparse autoencoders, enabling more targeted control and better preservation of generation quality.
papers.conclusion: SAE-SSV enables effective LLM steering by operating in sparse, task-specific subspaces, outperforming existing methods and providing a more targeted and interpretable approach to behavior control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-SSV consistently outperforms baseline steering methods (CAA, RePe, Top PC, ITI) in steering success rate across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity tasks.
A notably small subspace of SAE latent dimensions is sufficient for effective steering, enabling targeted and interpretable interventions.
Steering in the structured SAE subspace preserves or improves generation quality (lexical diversity, entropy) compared to baselines, which often degrade it.
The method generalizes to unseen datasets within the same task domain, capturing both semantic directions and stylistic patterns.
The top SAE features used for steering are interpretable and correspond to semantically meaningful concepts related to the target attribute.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to pretrained sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which may not be available for all models or domains.
Only evaluated on LLMs with up to 9B parameters; scaling to larger models is future work.
Evaluation focused on open-ended generation tasks with limited human evaluation; generalizability to more specialized domains remains to be explored.
future_direction: Achieve universal and style-invariant SSVs that generalize across datasets, tasks, and model families by curating diverse training corpora and developing objectives that encourage semantic steering while minimizing stylistic sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, but controlling their behavior reliably remains challenging, especially in open-ended generation settings. This paper introduces a novel supervised steering approach that operates in sparse, interpretable representation spaces. We employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to obtain sparse latent representations that aim to disentangle semantic attributes from model activations. Then we train linear classifiers to identify a small subspace of task-relevant dimensions in latent representations. Finally, we learn supervised steering vectors constrained to this subspace, optimized to align with target behaviors. Experiments across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity steering tasks with multiple LLMs demonstrate that our supervised steering vectors achieve higher success rates with minimal degradation in generation quality compared to existing methods. Further analysis reveals that a notably small subspace is sufficient for effective steering, enabling more targeted and interpretable interventions. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Ineedanamehere/SAE-SSV.

papers.title: Activation Steering with a Feedback Controller
papers.research_question: How can we develop a control-theoretic foundation for activation steering in large language models to achieve more robust and reliable behavioral control?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes PID Steering, a control-theoretic framework for activation steering in LLMs that uses a Proportional-Integral-Derivative controller to compute steering vectors, reducing steady-state error and improving stability compared to existing methods.
papers.conclusion: PID Steering provides a principled control-theoretic framework for activation steering, offering improved performance, stability, and interpretability for controlling LLM behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Existing activation steering methods (ActAdd, DirAblate, Mean-AcT) correspond to proportional (P) controllers and suffer from steady-state error.
PID Steering reduces steady-state error and overshoot by incorporating integral and derivative terms.
PID Steering outperforms existing methods in toxicity mitigation and jailbreaking tasks across multiple model families and scales.
The method is lightweight, modular, and integrates with existing steering paradigms.
Theoretical analysis shows PID Steering ensures input-to-state stability and reduces the first-overshoot amplitude.
papers.abstract: Controlling the behaviors of large language models (LLM) is fundamental to their safety alignment and reliable deployment. However, existing steering methods are primarily driven by empirical insights and lack theoretical performance guarantees. In this work, we develop a control-theoretic foundation for activation steering by showing that popular steering methods correspond to the proportional (P) controllers, with the steering vector serving as the feedback signal. Building on this finding, we propose Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) Steering, a principled framework that leverages the full PID controller for activation steering in LLMs. The proportional (P) term aligns activations with target semantic directions, the integral (I) term accumulates errors to enforce persistent corrections across layers, and the derivative (D) term mitigates overshoot by counteracting rapid activation changes. This closed-loop design yields interpretable error dynamics and connects activation steering to classical stability guarantees in control theory. Moreover, PID Steering is lightweight, modular, and readily integrates with state-of-the-art steering methods. Extensive experiments across multiple LLM families and benchmarks demonstrate that PID Steering consistently outperforms existing approaches, achieving more robust and reliable behavioral control.

papers.title: Fine-tuned network relies on generic representation to solve unseen cognitive task
papers.research_question: When a pretrained language model is fine-tuned on a novel task, does it rely more on generic pretrained representations or develop brand new task-specific solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuned models rely heavily on pretrained representations (especially in later layers) to solve a novel cognitive task, while models trained from scratch develop different, more task-specific mechanisms, highlighting the trade-offs between leveraging pretrained knowledge and developing specialized solutions.
papers.conclusion: While fine-tuned models benefit from pretrained representations for generalization and performance, models trained from scratch might offer more specialized and potentially efficient solutions for specific tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuned models achieve higher accuracy with fewer training samples and generalize well to prompts generated with different bounds.
Fine-tuned models depend on attention heads in later layers, which are likely crucial for generic language modeling and were developed during pretraining.
Models trained from scratch develop task-specific solutions, with significant performance drops upon ablating heads in the first layer, which appear to extract numerical information.
Hidden states in fine-tuned models exhibit mixed selectivity, where a single unit's activation can encode multiple independent task-relevant variables simultaneously.
The importance of specific attention heads for task performance is consistent across fine-tuned models with different hyperparameters.
papers.limitation:
Further investigation is needed to elucidate the exact mechanism by which models trained from scratch solve this task.
Conclusions are based on one cognitive task; further studies with more diverse cognitive tasks are required to understand how pretrained representations support task-specific fine-tuning.
Much of the current findings are based on qualitative observations, and the field requires new quantitative metrics to ensure scientific rigor.
future_direction: Further investigation into the exact mechanism by which models trained from scratch solve the task.
Studies with more diverse cognitive tasks to understand how pretrained representations support task-specific fine-tuning.
Development of new quantitative metrics to advance mechanistic interpretability in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pretrained language models has shown promising results on a wide range of tasks, but when encountering a novel task, do they rely more on generic pretrained representation, or develop brand new task-specific solutions? Here, we fine-tuned GPT-2 on a context-dependent decision-making task, novel to the model but adapted from neuroscience literature. We compared its performance and internal mechanisms to a version of GPT-2 trained from scratch on the same task. Our results show that fine-tuned models depend heavily on pretrained representations, particularly in later layers, while models trained from scratch develop different, more task-specific mechanisms. These findings highlight the advantages and limitations of pretraining for task generalization and underscore the need for further investigation into the mechanisms underpinning task-specific fine-tuning in LLMs.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between cross-lingual transferability and the components of reasoning tasks (knowledge retrieval vs. knowledge-free reasoning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-free reasoning capability transfers nearly perfectly across languages, whereas knowledge retrieval significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer, attributed to shared neural mechanisms for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.conclusion: The demand for knowledge retrieval significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer performance, while knowledge-free reasoning ability can be nearly fully transferred between languages, due to shared neural mechanisms for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge retrieval component significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer in reasoning tasks; more knowledge retrieval leads to lower transfer effectiveness.
Knowledge-free reasoning capability can be nearly perfectly transferred across languages after fine-tuning in one language.
Cross-lingual computational similarity (hidden states and neuron activation) is higher for knowledge-free reasoning than for knowledge retrieval, especially in middle layers.
Target language proficiency impacts transferability; improving proficiency enhances cross-lingual transfer for knowledge-free reasoning.
The model uses similar neurons for knowledge-free reasoning across languages, while knowledge is stored separately in different languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited model selection and language coverage, primarily relying on LLaMA-2 and only ten languages.
Depth of interpretability analysis is limited; macro-level numerical analyses without precisely identifying specific neurons.
future_direction: Conduct more detailed neuron-level analyses to verify hypotheses about shared neurons for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities across multiple languages. However, the relationship between capabilities in different languages is less explored. In this work, we decompose the process of reasoning tasks into two separated components: knowledge retrieval and knowledge-free reasoning, and analyze the relationship between cross-lingual transferability and these two components. With adapted commonsense reasoning datasets and constructed knowledge-free reasoning datasets, we show that the knowledge-free reasoning capability can be nearly perfectly transferred across various source-target language directions despite the secondary impact of resource in some specific target languages, while cross-lingual knowledge retrieval significantly hinders the transfer. Moreover, by analyzing the hidden states and feed-forward network neuron activation during the reasoning, we show that higher similarity of hidden representations and larger overlap of activated neurons could explain the better cross-lingual transferability of knowledge-free reasoning than knowledge retrieval. Thus, we hypothesize that knowledge-free reasoning shares similar neurons in different languages for reasoning, while knowledge is stored separately in different languages. Our code and data is available at: https://github.com/NJUNLP/Knowledge-Free-Reasoning.

papers.title: Scaling laws for activation steering with Llama 2 models and refusal mechanisms
papers.research_question: How does the effectiveness of the Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering technique scale with model size, specifically for controlling refusal behavior in Llama 2 models?
papers.core_contribution: The effectiveness of Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) for steering model behavior diminishes with increasing model size, negative steering is more effective than positive steering, and steering is most effective when applied at early-mid layers.
papers.conclusion: Model alignment is complex and requires nuanced approaches to steer models effectively as they become larger, with future research needed to understand the interplay between alignment strategies, model architecture, and dataset characteristics.
papers.key_findings:
CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers (approximately 0.4 × total layer count).
The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size, making larger models harder to steer with the same vectors.
Negative steering (towards non-refusal) has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.
The layer of peak steering effectiveness for positive and negative steering converges as model size increases.
The diminishing effectiveness might be because larger models 'drown out' the steering vector due to more downstream computation.
papers.limitation: The experiments were limited to the specific topic of refusal and the results may be different for different topics or prompting approaches.
future_direction: Feature steering with sparse autoencoders (SAE).
Modifying activation steering for larger models, e.g., scaling up steering vectors or injecting at multiple layers.
Experimenting with diverse model architectures (e.g., Mistral, BERT, BLOOM) to understand alignment differences.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve in complexity and capability, the efficacy of less widely deployed alignment techniques are uncertain. Building on previous work on activation steering and contrastive activation addition (CAA), this paper explores the effectiveness of CAA with model scale using the family of Llama 2 models (7B, 13B, and 70B). CAA works by finding desirable 'directions' in the model's residual stream vector space using contrastive pairs (for example, hate to love) and adding this direction to the residual stream during the forward pass. It directly manipulates the residual stream and aims to extract features from language models to better control their outputs. Using answer matching questions centered around the refusal behavior, we found that 1) CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers. 2) The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size. 3) Negative steering has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.

papers.title: To Steer or Not to Steer? Mechanistic Error Reduction with Abstention for Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively steer language models to mitigate errors by calibrating when and how much to steer, thereby avoiding under- and oversteering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MERA, a principled framework for error mitigation in language models via calibrated activation steering, which optimizes intervention direction and strength to provably improve performance or abstain.
papers.conclusion: MERA provides a safe, effective, and general-purpose framework for mechanistic activation steering that guarantees improved or non-degrading performance through calibrated interventions.
papers.key_findings:
MERA outperforms existing steering baselines across diverse models and tasks, providing safe and non-degrading error correction.
Steering based on the 'exact' token position (first token matching a valid label) generally performs as well as or better than the traditional 'last' token position.
Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features do not consistently improve probe performance for error estimation compared to original activations.
MERA can be applied on top of existing steering techniques (e.g., contrastive or probe-based) to further enhance their performance.
The calibration step in MERA ensures interventions are only applied when they are confidently beneficial, preventing performance degradation.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) classification tasks, which may not reflect performance in more complex, open-ended generation tasks.
Steering for specialized error correction might inadvertently impair the model's general capabilities or text fluency.
future_direction: Extend MERA to alignment objectives such as toxicity reduction, refusal behavior, and harmfulness mitigation.
Replace linear error probes with non-linear estimators (e.g., neural networks).
Investigate the impact of using different evaluation metrics (e.g., F1 score) during calibration for tasks with class imbalance.
papers.abstract: We introduce Mechanistic Error Reduction with Abstention (MERA), a principled framework for steering language models (LMs) to mitigate errors through selective, adaptive interventions. Unlike existing methods that rely on fixed, manually tuned steering strengths, often resulting in under or oversteering, MERA addresses these limitations by (i) optimising the intervention direction, and (ii) calibrating when, and how much to steer, thereby provably improving performance or abstaining when no confident correction is possible. Experiments across diverse datasets, and LM families demonstrate safe, effective, non-degrading error correction, and that MERA outperforms existing baselines. Moreover, MERA can be applied on top of existing steering techniques to further enhance their performance, establishing it as a general-purpose, and efficient approach to mechanistic activation steering.

papers.title: Contextual Feature Extraction Hierarchies Converge in Large Language Models and the Brain
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with the brain's language processing mechanisms, and do LLMs share fundamental computational principles that increasingly align with the spoken language processing pathway in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that higher-performing large language models (LLMs) exhibit greater alignment with the brain's hierarchical language processing, and that contextual information is a key factor driving this convergence.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that hierarchical structure and contextual dependencies are fundamental to language processing, leading to convergent strategies in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-performing LLMs achieve higher peak brain similarity scores.
Better-performing LLMs peak in brain similarity at earlier layers compared to lower-performing models.
Better-performing LLMs have hierarchical feature extraction pathways that more closely align with the brain's hierarchy.
Contextual information is crucial for brain similarity and hierarchy alignment, with long context windows being particularly important.
Top-performing LLMs converge in their feature extraction hierarchies, as shown by high inter-model similarity.
papers.limitation:
Limited iEEG coverage may not capture all relevant brain regions.
The speech comprehension task is simple and may not fully engage higher-level language processing.
LLMs are trained for next-word prediction, which differs from the comprehension task performed by subjects.
future_direction: Using brain similarity as an evaluation metric for LLM development.
Improving contextual processing in LLMs to enhance performance and brain alignment.
Investigating the role of later layers in LLMs for higher-order integration.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have sparked interest in the parallels between large language models (LLMs) and human neural processing, particularly in language comprehension. While prior research has established similarities in the representation of LLMs and the brain, the underlying computational principles that cause this convergence, especially in the context of evolving LLMs, remain elusive. Here, we examined a diverse selection of high-performance LLMs with similar parameter sizes to investigate the factors contributing to their alignment with the brain's language processing mechanisms. We find that as LLMs achieve higher performance on benchmark tasks, they not only become more brain-like as measured by higher performance when predicting neural responses from LLM embeddings, but also their hierarchical feature extraction pathways map more closely onto the brain's while using fewer layers to do the same encoding. We also compare the feature extraction pathways of the LLMs to each other and identify new ways in which high-performing models have converged toward similar hierarchical processing mechanisms. Finally, we show the importance of contextual information in improving model performance and brain similarity. Our findings reveal the converging aspects of language processing in the brain and LLMs and offer new directions for developing models that align more closely with human cognitive processing.

papers.title: Ability Transfer and Recovery via Modularized Parameters Localization
papers.research_question: How are abilities distributed within LLM parameters? The paper investigates this by analyzing module activations under domain- and language-specific inputs for closely related models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ACT, a method that localizes ability-relevant channels in LLMs via cross-model activation differences and selectively transfers only the corresponding parameters, enabling efficient ability transfer and recovery while minimizing interference.
papers.conclusion: ACT enables efficient and effective ability transfer and recovery by localizing and transferring modularized ability-relevant parameters, and it can integrate multiple abilities into a single model with minimal interference.
papers.key_findings:
Large activation differences are concentrated in a small fraction of channels (typically <5%).
Activation difference distributions across different layers exhibit consistent heavy-tailed patterns.
Ability-specific channels are naturally disentangled across different language-domain abilities.
Ability-specific channels exhibit consistency after fine-tuning across different fine-tuned variants.
Ability-specific channels selected by activations differ from largely updated ones during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes the availability of a base model and an ability model that share the same architecture and tokenizer, and are preferably derived from the same pretrained checkpoint.
The effectiveness of ACT may be limited when the parameter drift between the base and ability models is too large, as observed in some continuous pre-training scenarios.
future_direction: Extending ACT to more diverse abilities and tasks beyond reasoning domains.
Exploring the theoretical foundations of activation-based ability localization.
Applying ACT to other model families and architectures beyond transformers.
papers.abstract: Large language models can be continually pre-trained or fine-tuned to improve performance in specific domains, languages, or skills, but this specialization often degrades other capabilities and may cause catastrophic forgetting. We investigate how abilities are distributed within LLM parameters by analyzing module activations under domain- and language-specific inputs for closely related models. Across layers and modules, we find that ability-related activations are highly concentrated in a small set of channels (typically <5\%), and these channels are largely disentangled with good sufficiency and stability. Building on these observations, we propose ACT (Activation-Guided Channel-wise Ability Transfer), which localizes ability-relevant channels via activation differences and selectively transfers only the corresponding parameters, followed by lightweight fine-tuning for compatibility. Experiments on multilingual mathematical and scientific reasoning show that ACT can recover forgotten abilities while preserving retained skills. It can also merge multiple specialized models to integrate several abilities into a single model with minimal interference. Our code and data will be publicly released.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: DESTEIN: Navigating Detoxification of Language Models via Universal Steering Pairs and Head-wise Activation Fusion
papers.research_question: How can we detoxify language models efficiently with lower resource and time costs by using representation engineering in activation spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DESTEIN, a novel method for detoxifying language models via representation engineering in activation spaces using self-induced universal steering pairs and head-wise activation fusion, achieving state-of-the-art detoxification with lower computational cost while maintaining generation quality.
papers.conclusion: DESTEIN is an effective, scalable, and efficient method for detoxifying language models without fine-tuning, preserving generative capabilities and offering a new perspective for controllable generation in activation spaces.
papers.key_findings:
DESTEIN outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods in detoxification metrics (EMT and TP) while maintaining fluency and diversity.
The method is scalable across various LLMs (GPT2, LLaMA2, OPT, MPT) of different sizes.
The use of self-induced parallel steering pairs and head-wise activation fusion with probing weights is effective for detoxification.
DESTEIN exhibits a better trade-off between detoxification strength and fluency compared to previous methods, avoiding generative collapse.
The method maintains task performance on the MMLU benchmark after detoxification, similar to parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the linear representation assumption, which is an approximation and may not hold completely.
Constructing ideal parallel steering pairs is difficult.
The method is an indirect form of decoupling and faces theoretical challenges in achieving complete separation of toxic attributes and general capabilities.
future_direction: Explore more efficient and versatile decoupling strategies such as causal reasoning, knowledge guidance, or meta-learning techniques.
Integrate the method with toxicity classifiers to achieve better results by applying detoxification selectively.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable achievements of language models (LMs) across a broad spectrum of tasks, their propensity for generating toxic outputs remains a prevalent concern. Current solutions involving finetuning or auxiliary models usually require extensive computational resources, hindering their practicality in large language models (LLMs). In this paper, we propose DeStein, a novel method that detoxifies LMs by applying representation engineering in activation spaces with lower resource and time costs. Specifically, we derive detoxification vectors from self-induced, universal steering pairs through arithmetic operations in activation spaces. During inference, detoxification is achieved by fusing the detoxification vectors with the original representations in a head-wise manner. Empirical results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches on various metrics, while also maintaining satisfactory generation quality and diversity. We further validate the practicality and scalability of DeStein with a series of white-box LLMs. The method is open-sourced at https://github.com/LizLizLi/DeStein. Warning: Some example model outputs may contain highly offensive or disturbing text.

papers.title: On the Limitations of Steering in Language Model Alignment
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of steering vectors as alignment mechanisms in language models, particularly with respect to prompt structure and context complexity?
papers.core_contribution: Steering vectors are promising for specific alignment tasks like value alignment but may not provide a robust foundation for general-purpose alignment in LLMs, particularly in complex scenarios.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors show promise for aligning language model behavior, particularly in tasks like bias mitigation and value alignment, but they struggle with consistency in complex, socially sensitive contexts and can introduce factual inaccuracies through overcorrection.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors can reduce bias in sensitive scenarios, such as hiring decisions.
Steering vectors can lead to overcorrection, causing factual inaccuracies, as seen in a legal case.
Steering vectors can introduce inconsistencies in complex, multi-faceted contexts, such as a student election.
The effectiveness of steering vectors depends on prompt structure and context complexity.
Causal analysis can identify high-leverage intervention points (layers) for applying steering vectors.
papers.limitation:
Steering can lead to overcorrection, causing factual distortions.
Steering introduces inconsistencies in complex contexts requiring multi-faceted reasoning.
Steering may not provide a robust foundation for general-purpose alignment.
future_direction: Explore how architectural variations across models affect the reliability and limits of steering-based alignment.
Extend the proof of concept to reasoning or instruction-tuned models.
Develop more dynamic and context-sensitive steering mechanisms that adapt to nuanced social cues without compromising factual consistency.
Generalize the proof of concept into scalable, plug-and-play alignment tools for high-stakes domains.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a promising approach to aligning language model behavior at inference time. In this paper, we propose a framework to assess the limitations of steering vectors as alignment mechanisms. Using a framework of transformer hook interventions and antonym-based function vectors, we evaluate the role of prompt structure and context complexity in steering effectiveness. Our findings indicate that steering vectors are promising for specific alignment tasks, such as value alignment, but may not provide a robust foundation for general-purpose alignment in LLMs, particularly in complex scenarios. We establish a methodological foundation for future investigations into steering capabilities of reasoning models.

papers.title: Uncovering Latent Chain of Thought Vectors in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors derived from LM activations induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning without natural language prompting?
papers.core_contribution: Steering vectors derived from contrastive activations can induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning in frozen language models, matching or exceeding the performance of traditional CoT prompting.
papers.conclusion: Steering vector injection can effectively induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning in language models without prompting, suggesting reasoning capabilities are encoded in activation and weight space. The method matches or exceeds CoT prompting performance, with injection timing influencing results.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vector injection induces CoT reasoning without natural language prompts.
The method achieves competitive or superior performance compared to CoT prompting on GSM8k, MMLU, ARC AI2, and AGI Eval benchmarks.
The approach generalizes to unseen data, as shown on the SAT Math section of AGI Eval.
Different injection strategies (single vs. continuous) yield varying performance across benchmarks.
Steered models produce more structured, step-by-step reasoning outputs while retaining natural language fluency.
papers.limitation: Performance varies with injection strategy and may not be optimized.
future_direction: Explore different methods for injecting steering vectors to optimize performance and reliability
Investigate generalization capabilities of steering vectors across different models
Scale up the approach to larger models
papers.abstract: In this work, we examine how targeted perturbations in the activation space of Language Models (LMs) can encode complex reasoning patterns. We inject steering vectors, derived from LM activations, into LMs during inference time and study whether these vectors can induce Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LMs without the need for natural language prompting. We demonstrate this approach on Llama3 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B v0.2 Instruct and show that activation-space interventions achieve competitive, if not superior, performance compared to traditional CoT prompting across multiple reasoning benchmarks, including GSM8k, MMLU, AGI Eval, and ARC AI2. These findings suggest that neural network activations can encode reasoning patterns, offering a new application of activation space manipulation as a tool for tuning model behavior.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Improved Representation Steering for Language Models
papers.research_question: How can representation steering for language models be improved to provide fine-grained, interpretable control over model generations, particularly to narrow the performance gap with prompting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Reference-free Preference Steering (RePS), a bidirectional preference-optimization objective for training intervention-based steering methods, which outperforms existing methods and narrows the performance gap with prompting while being interpretable and robust to jailbreaking attacks.
papers.conclusion: RePS provides an interpretable and robust alternative to prompting for both steering and suppression of concepts in language models.
papers.key_findings:
RePS-trained interventions consistently outperform the standard language modeling objective and the prior BiPO baseline on the AXBENCH benchmark across Gemma models from 2B to 27B parameters.
RePS narrows the performance gap between representation steering and prompting-based methods for concept steering.
For concept suppression, RePS performs on par with the language modeling objective on smaller models and outperforms it on larger Gemma-3 models.
RePS-trained models remain resilient to prompt-based jailbreaking attacks that bypass text-prompt defenses, whereas prompting-based strategies often fail.
The method is effective with low-rank parameterizations including steering vectors, LoRA, and ReFT, promoting interpretability and minimizing parameter count.
papers.abstract: Steering methods for language models (LMs) seek to provide fine-grained and interpretable control over model generations by variously changing model inputs, weights, or representations to adjust behavior. Recent work has shown that adjusting weights or representations is often less effective than steering by prompting, for instance when wanting to introduce or suppress a particular concept. We demonstrate how to improve representation steering via our new Reference-free Preference Steering (RePS), a bidirectional preference-optimization objective that jointly does concept steering and suppression. We train three parameterizations of RePS and evaluate them on AxBench, a large-scale model steering benchmark. On Gemma models with sizes ranging from 2B to 27B, RePS outperforms all existing steering methods trained with a language modeling objective and substantially narrows the gap with prompting -- while promoting interpretability and minimizing parameter count. In suppression, RePS matches the language-modeling objective on Gemma-2 and outperforms it on the larger Gemma-3 variants while remaining resilient to prompt-based jailbreaking attacks that defeat prompting. Overall, our results suggest that RePS provides an interpretable and robust alternative to prompting for both steering and suppression.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters.
