However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: On the generalization capacity of neural networks during generic multimodal reasoning
papers.research_question: How do different neural network architectures generalize on three types of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in multimodal reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the gCOG benchmark for evaluating multimodal OOD generalization and shows that cross-attention and deeper attention layers improve distractor and systematic generalization, but not productive generalization.
papers.conclusion: Cross-attention and deeper attention layers are key for distractor and systematic generalization, but productive generalization remains a fundamental challenge for current neural architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Models with cross-attention mechanisms (CrossAttn and Perceiver) performed best on distractor generalization.
Cross-attention models also performed best on systematic compositional generalization.
All models failed on productive compositional generalization.
Increasing layer depth and attention heads in Transformers improved distractor and systematic generalization but not productive generalization.
Representation analysis showed that better performing models retained more stimulus and response information in their penultimate layer.
papers.limitation: Existing neural architectures fail to exhibit productive compositional generalization.
future_direction: Identifying neural architectures capable of performing multimodal OOD generalization.
Using the gCOG benchmark for future studies.
papers.abstract: The advent of the Transformer has led to the development of large language models (LLM), which appear to demonstrate human-like capabilities. To assess the generality of this class of models and a variety of other base neural network architectures to multimodal domains, we evaluated and compared their capacity for multimodal generalization. We introduce a multimodal question-answer benchmark to evaluate three specific types of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization performance: distractor generalization (generalization in the presence of distractors), systematic compositional generalization (generalization to new task permutations), and productive compositional generalization (generalization to more complex tasks structures). We found that across model architectures (e.g., RNNs, Transformers, Perceivers, etc.), models with multiple attention layers, or models that leveraged cross-attention mechanisms between input domains, fared better. Our positive results demonstrate that for multimodal distractor and systematic generalization, either cross-modal attention or models with deeper attention layers are key architectural features required to integrate multimodal inputs. On the other hand, neither of these architectural features led to productive generalization, suggesting fundamental limitations of existing architectures for specific types of multimodal generalization. These results demonstrate the strengths and limitations of specific architectural components underlying modern neural models for multimodal reasoning. Finally, we provide Generic COG (gCOG), a configurable benchmark with several multimodal generalization splits, for future studies to explore.

papers.title: Distribution-Aligned Decoding for Efficient LLM Task Adaptation
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently adapt large language models to downstream tasks by directly aligning the output distribution during decoding, instead of through weight updates?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Steering Vector Decoding (SVDecode), a lightweight, PEFT-compatible method for task adaptation that steers the model's output distribution towards the task distribution directly during decoding, without adding trainable parameters beyond the PEFT adapter.
papers.conclusion: SVDecode offers a lightweight, theoretically grounded, and effective path to stronger task adaptation for large language models by directly aligning output distributions during decoding.
papers.key_findings:
SVDecode consistently improves multiple-choice accuracy (up to 5 points) and open-ended truthfulness (up to 2 points) across various models and PEFT methods.
The method is theoretically grounded, being first-order equivalent to the gradient step of full fine-tuning, and an analytical solution for the optimal steering strength is derived.
SVDecode operates during decoding without requiring backward passes, making it computationally efficient and compatible with any existing PEFT method.
A confidence-aware constraint and logit-space projection are crucial for stable and robust performance, preventing issues from low-probability tokens.
The method demonstrates generalizability, showing performance gains on commonsense reasoning tasks (1-2 point average improvement) without task-specific retuning.
papers.limitation: SVDecode depends on an initial warm-start fine-tuning phase to identify an effective, task-specific steering direction, which requires labeled data and computational resources.
future_direction: Exploring the development of label-free or retrieval-augmented approaches capable of deriving robust steering vectors directly from unlabelled corpora, eliminating the warm-start requirement.
papers.abstract: Adapting billion-parameter language models to a downstream task is still costly, even with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). We re-cast task adaptation as output-distribution alignment: the objective is to steer the output distribution toward the task distribution directly during decoding rather than indirectly through weight updates. Building on this view, we introduce Steering Vector Decoding (SVDecode), a lightweight, PEFT-compatible, and theoretically grounded method. We start with a short warm-start fine-tune and extract a task-aware steering vector from the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence gradient between the output distribution of the warm-started and pre-trained models. This steering vector is then used to guide the decoding process to steer the model's output distribution towards the task distribution. We theoretically prove that SVDecode is first-order equivalent to the gradient step of full fine-tuning and derive a globally optimal solution for the strength of the steering vector. Across three tasks and nine benchmarks, SVDecode paired with four standard PEFT methods improves multiple-choice accuracy by up to 5 percentage points and open-ended truthfulness by 2 percentage points, with similar gains (1-2 percentage points) on commonsense datasets without adding trainable parameters beyond the PEFT adapter. SVDecode thus offers a lightweight, theoretically grounded path to stronger task adaptation for large language models. Code is available at https://github.com/dl-m9/SVDecode.

papers.title: REAL: Reading Out Transformer Activations for Precise Localization in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we better identify internal modules (attention heads or layers) that govern specific behaviors in LLMs for the purpose of inference-time steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REAL, a framework that uses a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) to learn a disentangled latent space from module activations, enabling more precise identification of behavior-relevant modules (heads or layers) for inference-time steering in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: REAL provides a more effective and principled approach for selecting behavior-relevant modules in Transformers, leading to improved performance across a variety of inference-time steering tasks including truthfulness enhancement, knowledge conflict resolution, and general alignment.
papers.key_findings:
REAL outperforms existing methods like ITI and LoFiT in truthfulness steering, achieving significant improvements (e.g., up to 81.5% relative improvement on MC1 for Qwen2.5-7B).
The attention heads selected by REAL on a truthfulness task show strong zero-shot generalization to knowledge-seeking tasks in different model families.
REAL effectively localizes layers for steering in knowledge conflict tasks, outperforming the state-of-the-art SPARE method on benchmarks like NQSWAP and MACNOISE.
The method's relevance scores, derived from the VQ-AE encodings, provide a principled way to rank modules and assign steering strengths.
Visualizations (t-SNE, heatmaps) show that REAL identifies heads with more discriminative activation patterns compared to linear-probe-based methods.
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering aims to alter a large language model's (LLM's) responses without changing its parameters, but a central challenge is identifying the internal modules that most strongly govern the target behavior. Existing approaches often rely on simplistic cues or ad hoc heuristics, leading to suboptimal or unintended effects. We introduce REAL, a framework for identifying behavior-relevant modules (attention heads or layers) in Transformer models. For each module, REAL trains a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) on its hidden activations and uses a shared, learnable codebook to partition the latent space into behavior-relevant and behavior-irrelevant subspaces. REAL quantifies a module's behavioral relevance by how well its VQ-AE encodings discriminate behavior-aligned from behavior-violating responses via a binary classification metric; this score guides both module selection and steering strength. We evaluate REAL across eight LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families and nine datasets spanning truthfulness enhancement, open-domain QA under knowledge conflicts, and general alignment tasks. REAL enables more effective inference-time interventions, achieving an average relative improvement of 20% (up to 81.5%) over the ITI method on truthfulness steering. In addition, the modules selected by REAL exhibit strong zero-shot generalization in cross-domain truthfulness-steering scenarios.

papers.title: Exploring and Exploiting the Inherent Efficiency within Large Reasoning Models for Self-Guided Efficiency Enhancement
papers.research_question: Can the inherent efficiency within large reasoning models be exploited to reduce overthinking and enhance reasoning efficiency without compromising performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that large reasoning models inherently possess untapped efficiency potential, and proposes two self-guided methods—Efficiency Steering (a training-free activation steering technique) and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL (a reinforcement learning framework)—that significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance.
papers.conclusion: Overthinking in large reasoning models is a controllable behavior embedded in internal representations; the proposed self-guided methods (Efficiency Steering and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL) successfully enhance reasoning efficiency without external supervision, offering practical directions for building more cost-efficient reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
LRMs exhibit inherent efficiency: the shortest correct reasoning paths are often less than half the length of the longest correct ones, indicating substantial untapped efficiency potential.
Efficient and verbose reasoning paths are linearly separable in the model's representation space, with consistent positional shifts across layers and difficulty levels.
Efficiency Steering, a training-free method that injects a single vector direction derived from contrastive reasoning pairs, can controllably modulate reasoning length without compromising accuracy.
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, which uses a dynamic reward function balancing correctness and brevity, significantly reduces reasoning length while maintaining or slightly improving accuracy across multiple benchmarks.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on simpler mathematical problems (Levels 1-3) leads to efficient reasoning that transfers well to harder problems, suggesting that efficiency priors learned from simple data are effective.
papers.limitation:
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL is sensitive to optimization steps; beyond 30 steps, efficiency improves but correctness can deteriorate, indicating a trade-off that requires careful tuning.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on harder mathematical examples (Levels 4-5) does not yield as favorable efficiency outcomes as training on simpler examples, suggesting that data distribution impacts the method's effectiveness.
future_direction: Further exploration of representational properties of LLMs to build efficiency-aware alignment strategies with minimal external supervision.
Investigating curriculum-aware or simplicity-biased training strategies for self-rewarded efficiency optimization, as simpler problems may provide better efficiency outcomes at lower training cost.
Refining the capabilities that already exist within LRMs for building more efficient and accessible reasoning systems.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large reasoning models (LRMs) have significantly enhanced language models' capabilities in complex problem-solving by emulating human-like deliberative thinking. However, these models often exhibit overthinking (i.e., the generation of unnecessarily verbose and redundant content), which hinders efficiency and inflates inference cost. In this work, we explore the representational and behavioral origins of this inefficiency, revealing that LRMs inherently possess the capacity for more concise reasoning. Empirical analyses show that correct reasoning paths vary significantly in length, and the shortest correct responses often suffice, indicating untapped efficiency potential. Exploiting these findings, we propose two lightweight methods to enhance LRM efficiency. First, we introduce Efficiency Steering, a training-free activation steering technique that modulates reasoning behavior via a single direction in the model's representation space. Second, we develop Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, a reinforcement learning framework that dynamically balances task accuracy and brevity by rewarding concise correct solutions. Extensive experiments on seven LRM backbones across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our methods significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance. Our results highlight that reasoning efficiency can be improved by leveraging and guiding the intrinsic capabilities of existing models in a self-guided manner.

papers.title: Controlling Large Language Model Agents with Entropic Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How do LLM agents explore, and how can we control their exploratory behaviors? How can we effectively intervene on overconfident behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Entropic Activation Steering (EAST), a method to control LLM agents' exploration and uncertainty by steering activations, showing that LLMs encode uncertainty in their representation space.
papers.conclusion: Our work paves the way for a new understanding of the functioning of LLM agents and to effective control of their decision-making behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
EAST can effectively manipulate an LLM agent's exploration by directly affecting the high-level actions parsed from the LLM outputs.
EAST modulates the uncertainty exhibited in the LLM's thoughts, guiding the agent towards more exploratory actions.
The steering vectors obtained by EAST generalize across task variants.
LLM agents explicitly encode uncertainty over their actions in their representation space.
EAST increases action entropy and affects subjective uncertainty, steering away from overconfidence.
papers.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has prompted increasing interest in their use as in-context learning agents. At the core of agentic behavior is the capacity for exploration, or the ability to actively gather information about the environment. But how do LLM agents explore, and how can we control their exploratory behaviors? To answer these questions, we take a representation-level perspective, and introduce Entropic Activation Steering (EAST), an activation steering method for in-context LLM agents. Firstly, we demonstrate that EAST can effectively manipulate an LLM agent's exploration by directly affecting the high-level actions parsed from the outputs of the LLM, in contrast to token-level temperature sampling. Secondly, we reveal how applying this control modulates the uncertainty exhibited in the LLM's thoughts, guiding the agent towards more exploratory actions. Finally, we demonstrate that the steering vectors obtained by EAST generalize across task variants. In total, these results show that LLM agents explicitly encode uncertainty over their actions in their representation space. Our work paves the way for a new understanding of the functioning of LLM agents and to effective control of their decision-making behaviors.

papers.title: Steering When Necessary: Flexible Steering Large Language Models with Backtracking
papers.research_question: How to dynamically determine the necessity and strength of intervention when steering large language models, and how to correct deviated tokens through backtracking?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a flexible activation steering framework with backtracking that dynamically determines intervention necessity and strength by tracking LLM internal states, and a backtracking mechanism to correct deviated tokens.
papers.conclusion: The FASB framework effectively steers LLMs by dynamically determining intervention necessity and strength, with backtracking correcting deviated tokens, and demonstrates strong performance across multiple tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
FASB outperforms existing activation steering baselines on TruthfulQA and multiple-choice datasets.
Ablation studies show that adaptive intervention strength and the backtracking mechanism are crucial for performance.
The method generalizes to various LLMs of different sizes and architectures, and to out-of-distribution truthful benchmarks.
Performance improves with more attention heads and higher intervention strength, but informativeness may degrade with excessive intervention.
The method is effective even with limited training data for the probe.
papers.limitation:
The method may be used for malicious purposes (e.g., jailbreaking, toxic content generation).
The approach is hyperparameter-dependent and focused on QA tasks for specific behaviors (truthfulness, informativeness) on English datasets.
Evaluation uses LLM-based judges which may introduce errors.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many generation tasks. Nevertheless, effectively aligning them with desired behaviors remains a significant challenge. Activation steering is an effective and cost-efficient approach that directly modifies the activations of LLMs during the inference stage, aligning their responses with the desired behaviors and avoiding the high cost of fine-tuning. Existing methods typically indiscriminately intervene to all generations or rely solely on the question to determine intervention, which limits the accurate assessment of the intervention strength. To this end, we propose the Flexible Activation Steering with Backtracking (FASB) framework, which dynamically determines both the necessity and strength of intervention by tracking the internal states of the LLMs during generation, considering both the question and the generated content. Since intervening after detecting a deviation from the desired behavior is often too late, we further propose the backtracking mechanism to correct the deviated tokens and steer the LLMs toward the desired behavior. Extensive experiments on the TruthfulQA dataset and six multiple-choice datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms baselines. Our code will be released at https://github.com/gjw185/FASB.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: STU-PID: Steering Token Usage via PID Controller for Efficient Large Language Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be dynamically controlled to suppress redundant reasoning chunks in LLMs without harming accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STU-PID, a training-free decoding-time method that uses a PID controller to dynamically adjust activation steering based on chunk-level redundancy, improving both accuracy and token efficiency in reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: STU-PID effectively turns activation steering into a closed-loop control problem, achieving simultaneous improvements in accuracy and token savings on math reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
STU-PID improves accuracy from 85.7% to 89.6% and reduces average output length from 1026 to 790 tokens on a GSM8K subset with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B.
Adaptive steering via PID controller avoids the accuracy-token trade-off seen with fixed-coefficient methods like SEAL.
The method requires only a small linear classifier and PID gains tuning, making it efficient and training-free for the main model.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to 77 problems, one dataset (GSM8K), and one 1.5B model, so results are a proof of concept.
The redundancy classifier is trained on math chunks and may not transfer to non-math reasoning without new labels.
PID gains and target probability were tuned by hand, and behavior under automated tuning or larger models is not characterized.
No ablation of individual PID terms, so the contribution of each term is unknown.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and non-math reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models employing extended chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning often suffer from the overthinking phenomenon, generating excessive and redundant reasoning steps that increase computational costs while potentially degrading performance. While recent work has explored static steering approaches to mitigate this issue, they lack the adaptability to dynamically adjust intervention strength based on real-time reasoning quality. We propose STUPID (Steering Token Usage via PID controller), a novel training-free method that employs a PID controller to dynamically modulate activation steering strength during inference. Our approach combines a chunk-level classifier for detecting redundant reasoning patterns with a PID control mechanism that adaptively adjusts steering intensity based on the predicted redundancy probability. Experimental evaluation on GSM8K demonstrates that STUPID achieves a 6% improvement in accuracy while reducing token usage by 32%, outperforming static steering baselines. Our method provides a principled framework for dynamic reasoning calibration that maintains reasoning quality while significantly improving computational efficiency.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: ODESteer: A Unified ODE-Based Steering Framework for LLM Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we develop a unified theoretical framework for activation steering in LLM alignment that addresses the limitations of one-step steering and lack of theoretical guidance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a unified ODE-based theoretical framework for activation steering in LLM alignment and introduces ODESTEER, a multi-step adaptive steering method that improves performance on alignment benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Establishes a principled new view of activation steering in LLM alignment by unifying theoretical foundations via ODEs and validating it empirically with ODESTEER.
papers.key_findings:
ODESTEER achieves consistent empirical improvements on diverse LLM alignment benchmarks, e.g., 5.7% on TruthfulQA, 2.5% on UltraFeedback, and 2.4% on RealToxicityPrompts.
Activation addition can be interpreted as a first-order approximation to the solution of an ODE.
Steering direction identification is equivalent to designing a barrier function from control theory.
ODESTEER enables multi-step and adaptive steering, capturing complex activation patterns better than one-step methods.
The method generalizes well across different models and tasks.
papers.limitation: Does not incorporate unsupervised feature learning methods into the proposed framework.
future_direction: Investigate integration of unsupervised feature learning into the ODE-based unified framework.
papers.abstract: Activation steering, or representation engineering, offers a lightweight approach to align large language models (LLMs) by manipulating their internal activations at inference time. However, current methods suffer from two key limitations: (i) the lack of a unified theoretical framework for guiding the design of steering directions, and (ii) an over-reliance on one-step steering that fail to capture complex patterns of activation distributions. In this work, we propose a unified ordinary differential equations (ODEs)-based theoretical framework for activation steering in LLM alignment. We show that conventional activation addition can be interpreted as a first-order approximation to the solution of an ODE. Based on this ODE perspective, identifying a steering direction becomes equivalent to designing a barrier function from control theory. Derived from this framework, we introduce ODESteer, a kind of ODE-based steering guided by barrier functions, which shows empirical advancement in LLM alignment. ODESteer identifies steering directions by defining the barrier function as the log-density ratio between positive and negative activations, and employs it to construct an ODE for multi-step and adaptive steering. Compared to state-of-the-art activation steering methods, ODESteer achieves consistent empirical improvements on diverse LLM alignment benchmarks, a notable $5.7\%$ improvement over TruthfulQA, $2.5\%$ over UltraFeedback, and $2.4\%$ over RealToxicityPrompts. Our work establishes a principled new view of activation steering in LLM alignment by unifying its theoretical foundations via ODEs, and validating it empirically through the proposed ODESteer method.

papers.title: Mitigating Memorization in LLMs using Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Can activation steering mitigate memorization in LLMs, and what factors influence its effectiveness? What are best practices for using activation steering to mitigate memorization?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can effectively reduce memorization in LLMs, especially when applied to later layers, with minimal impact on linguistic fluency and general performance.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering can suppress memorized content in LLMs while maintaining fluency and general abilities, offering a practical alternative to data sanitization or retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering reduces memorization, as shown by decreased ANLCS with high steering strength.
Steering later layers (e.g., Layer 31) minimizes degradation in language modeling and general task performance.
Early layer steering leads to significant performance drops in linguistic and reasoning tasks.
Random SAE features can be used for steering, indicating that memorization is distributed and not tied to specific features.
Features with high semantic footprint can cause stylistic shifts in output, which may be undesirable.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted only on the Gemma model.
The benchmark primarily consists of literary examples, which may have been present in the model's training data.
A more comprehensive evaluation incorporating diverse datasets and direct analysis of training data exposure is needed.
Future studies should assess the broader applicability of activation steering across different model architectures and tasks.
future_direction: More comprehensive evaluation with diverse datasets and direct analysis of training data exposure.
Assess broader applicability across different model architectures and tasks.
Explore more adaptive and dynamic steering mechanisms to enhance robustness while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.abstract: The memorization of training data by Large Language Models (LLMs) poses significant risks, including privacy leaks and the regurgitation of copyrighted content. Activation steering, a technique that directly intervenes in model activations, has emerged as a promising approach for manipulating LLMs. In this work, we explore the effectiveness of activation steering in reducing memorization while preserving generalization capabilities. We conduct empirical evaluations using a controlled memorization benchmark of literary material and demonstrate that our method successfully suppresses memorized content with minimal degradation in model performance in Gemma. Additionally, we analyze the trade-offs between suppression effectiveness and linguistic fluency, highlighting the advantages and limitations of activation-based interventions. Our findings contribute to ongoing efforts in developing safer and more privacy-preserving LLMs by providing a practical and efficient mechanism to mitigate unintended memorization.

papers.title: Shifting Perspectives: Steering Vectors for Robust Bias Mitigation in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors effectively mitigate social biases in LLMs, and how do they compare to other bias mitigation methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that steering vectors, applied to model activations at inference time, are a lightweight and effective method for mitigating social biases in LLMs, outperforming prompting and Self-Debias with minimal impact on general model performance.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors offer a plug-and-play, interpretable, and computationally lightweight intervention for bias mitigation, achieving substantial bias reduction with minimal impact on core LLM performance.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors achieved average accuracy improvements of 12.8% on BBQ, 8.3% on CLEAR-Bias, and 1% on StereoSet.
Steering vectors outperformed prompting and Self-Debias in all cases, and outperformed fine-tuning in 12 out of 17 evaluations.
Steering vectors had the lowest negative impact on MMLU scores (3.9% decrease) compared to other bias mitigation methods tested.
Steering vectors trained on one bias-specific dataset (BBQ) transferred effectively to other tasks and datasets, demonstrating robustness and generalizability.
Linear separability analysis identified optimal intervention layers (13-14) for applying the steering vectors.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on a 7B parameter model, which may not fully capture emergent abilities related to bias observed in larger models.
MMLU may not capture all aspects of language understanding and reasoning; additional benchmarks would provide a more complete assessment.
future_direction: Explore different contrastive dataset structures for constructing steering vectors.
Investigate multi-dimensional steering by controlling along multiple PCA axes simultaneously.
Study cross-axis interactions (e.g., gender vs. race) to mitigate unintended cross-bias amplification.
Develop adaptive coefficient selection strategies to dynamically adjust steering strength per input.
Apply steering vectors to other forms of harmful behaviors (e.g., toxicity, misinformation) and assess real-world impact.
papers.abstract: We present a novel approach to bias mitigation in large language models (LLMs) by applying steering vectors to modify model activations in forward passes. We compute 8 steering vectors, each corresponding to a different social bias axis, such as age, gender, or race, on a training subset of the BBQ dataset and compare the effectiveness of these to 3 additional bias mitigation methods across 4 datasets. When optimized on the BBQ dataset, our individually tuned steering vectors achieve average improvements of 12.8% on BBQ, 8.3% on CLEAR-Bias, and 1% on StereoSet, and show improvements over prompting and Self-Debias in all cases, and improvements over fine-tuning in 12 out of 17 evaluations. In addition, steering vectors showed the lowest impact on MMLU scores of the four bias mitigation methods tested. The work presents the first systematic investigation of steering vectors for bias mitigation, and we demonstrate that they are a powerful and computationally efficient strategy for reducing bias in LLMs, with broader implications for enhancing AI safety.

papers.title: Extracting Latent Steering Vectors from Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we extract latent steering vectors from pretrained language models to control text generation without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that latent steering vectors can be extracted from frozen pretrained language models to control text generation, enabling tasks like sentence recovery, style transfer, and semantic similarity without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The results indicate that frozen pretrained language models can be controlled effectively through their latent steering space.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors can be extracted from frozen language models and added to hidden states to recover target sentences with near-perfect BLEU-4 scores.
Vector arithmetic in the latent steering space enables unsupervised sentiment transfer on Yelp, performing comparably to autoencoder-based models tailored for the task.
Distances between steering vectors reflect sentence similarity, outperforming extractive methods like averaged hidden states and GloVe vectors on STS-B.
The latent steering space is smooth and interpretable: interpolations between vectors yield meaningful sentences, and vectors cluster by sentence.
The method does not simply memorize sequences; recovery is better for natural sentences than for gibberish or shuffled tokens.
papers.limitation:
Fluency can be challenging for higher values of λ in style transfer, leading to repetition of words or phrases.
Sampling from the latent space by treating steering vectors as independent Gaussians does not reliably produce well-formed text.
The method may reflect biases present in the underlying language model and could be misused to generate toxic text.
papers.abstract: Prior work on controllable text generation has focused on learning how to control language models through trainable decoding, smartprompt design, or fine-tuning based on a desired objective. We hypothesize that the information needed to steer the model to generate a target sentence is already encoded within the model. Accordingly, we explore a different approach altogether: extracting latent vectors directly from pretrained language model decoders without fine-tuning. Experiments show that there exist steering vectors, which, when added to the hidden states of the language model, generate a target sentence nearly perfectly (> 99 BLEU) for English sentences from a variety of domains. We show that vector arithmetic can be used for unsupervised sentiment transfer on the Yelp sentiment benchmark, with performance comparable to models tailored to this task. We find that distances between steering vectors reflect sentence similarity when evaluated on a textual similarity benchmark (STS-B), outperforming pooled hidden states of models. Finally, we present an analysis of the intrinsic properties of the steering vectors. Taken together, our results suggest that frozen LMs can be effectively controlled through their latent steering space. 1

papers.title: CogSteer: Cognition-Inspired Selective Layer Intervention for Efficiently Steering Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can human cognitive indicators (eye movement measures) be used to understand and efficiently steer Large Language Models by selecting optimal layers for semantic intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CogSteer, a cognition-inspired framework that uses eye movement correlations to heuristically select optimal layers for efficient semantic steering in LLMs via selective layer intervention, improving interpretability and parameter efficiency.
papers.conclusion: CogSteer provides an interpretable and efficient selective layer intervention method for steering LLMs, achieving strong performance with reduced computational costs, contributing to safer and more efficient deployment.
papers.key_findings:
LLM hidden states exhibit a strong correlation with human gaze, peaking in middle layers, indicating a hierarchical progression from syntactic/semantic processing to integration and prediction.
LLMs function as both next-token predictors and reasoners, with advanced models like Llama2-7B showing enhanced reasoning capabilities across layers.
Selective layer intervention in the middle bucket achieves comparable or superior performance to full-layer intervention while significantly reducing parameters and training time.
Heuristic steering layer selection adapts to different tasks, e.g., optimal layers vary for toxification vs. detoxification.
The method is model-agnostic, validated on GPT-2, Llama2-7B, and Mistral-7B across understanding, reasoning, and generation tasks.
papers.limitation: Analysis focused on feed-forward network (FFN) blocks, not attention blocks.
future_direction: Explore the mechanisms of attention blocks in greater depth.
Conduct further eye movement studies on factual information processing to refine analysis of mature bucket layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance through pretraining on extensive data. This enables efficient adaptation to diverse downstream tasks. However, the lack of interpretability in their underlying mechanisms limits the ability to effectively steer LLMs for specific applications. In this work, we investigate the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs from a cognitive perspective using eye movement measures. Specifically, we analyze the layer-wise correlation between human cognitive indicators and LLM representations. Building on these insights, we propose a heuristic approach for selecting the optimal steering layer to modulate LLM semantics. To this end, we introduce an efficient selective layer intervention based on prominent parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, which conventionally adjust either all layers or only the final layer. Additionally, we present an implicit layer contrastive intervention during inference to steer LLMs away from toxic outputs. Extensive experiments on natural language understanding, reasoning, and generation tasks, conducted on GPT-2, Llama2-7B, and Mistral-7B, demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. As a model-agnostic framework, it enhances the interpretability of LLMs while improving efficiency for safe deployment.

papers.title: LinEAS: End-to-end Learning of Activation Steering with a Distributional Loss
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently control generative models by steering activations with a global distributional loss that requires low data and is modality-agnostic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LinEAS, a method for activation steering that uses a global distributional loss to jointly learn affine transformations across layers, enabling effective control with low data and automatic neuron selection via sparsity regularization.
papers.conclusion: LinEAS is an effective method for activation steering, offering improved controllability and robustness by learning lightweight interventions with a global distributional loss.
papers.key_findings:
LinEAS outperforms existing activation steering methods on toxicity mitigation in LLMs and style control in text-to-image models.
LinEAS requires only a handful of unpaired samples (e.g., 32) to be effective.
The global loss and joint optimization across layers lead to more robust interventions and better preservation of model utility.
Sparsity regularization allows automatic selection of neurons and layers, reducing the intervention support by 100x.
LinEAS provides a continuous intervention strength parameter, allowing fine-grained control.
papers.limitation: The method requires access to intermediate activations, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending LinEAS to other modalities and tasks.
Investigating the theoretical properties of the distributional loss.
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative models in daily life calls for efficient mechanisms to control their generation, to e.g., produce safe content or provide users with tools to explore style changes. Ideally, such mechanisms should require low volume of unpaired data (i.e., without explicit preference), and should be cheap, both at train and inference time, while preserving output quality. Recent research has shown that such mechanisms can be obtained by intervening exclusively on model activations, with the goal of correcting distributional differences between activations seen when using prompts from a source vs. a target set (e.g., toxic and non-toxic sentences). While cheap, these fast methods are inherently crude: their maps are tuned locally, not accounting for their impact on downstream layers, resulting in interventions that cause unintended shifts when used out-of-sample. We propose in this work linear end-to-end activation steering (LinEAS), an approach trained with a global loss that accounts simultaneously for all layer-wise distributional shifts. In addition to being more robust, the loss used to train LinEAS can be regularized with sparsifying norms, which can automatically carry out neuron selection. LinEAS only requires a handful of unpaired samples to be effective, and beats similar baselines on toxicity mitigation in language models, becoming competitive with oracle-dependent methods that have access to strong supervision. LinEAS is modality-agnostic and we empirically find that it outperforms existing activation steering methods at mitigating and including new concepts at the output of single-step text-to-image generation models.

papers.title: Beyond Linear Steering: Unified Multi-Attribute Control for Language Models
papers.research_question: How to control multiple behavioral attributes in large language models at inference time without the limitations of linear steering methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces K-Steering, a method for multi-attribute control in LLMs using a non-linear classifier and gradient-based interventions, outperforming linear baselines.
papers.conclusion: K-Steering is a unified approach that effectively controls multiple behavioral attributes in LLMs, outperforming existing linear methods.
papers.key_findings:
K-Steering outperforms baseline methods like CAA and DCT in steering multiple attributes.
It avoids linearity assumptions and handles inter-attribute interactions robustly.
Multi-layer steering enhances effectiveness for complex tasks.
Multi-step steering improves performance with appropriate step sizes.
Projection removal using gradients efficiently ablates undesired attributes.
papers.limitation: Multi-step steering with large step sizes can degrade model outputs.
papers.abstract: Controlling multiple behavioral attributes in large language models (LLMs) at inference time is a challenging problem due to interference between attributes and the limitations of linear steering methods, which assume additive behavior in activation space and require per-attribute tuning. We introduce K-Steering, a unified and flexible approach that trains a single non-linear multi-label classifier on hidden activations and computes intervention directions via gradients at inference time. This avoids linearity assumptions, removes the need for storing and tuning separate attribute vectors, and allows dynamic composition of behaviors without retraining. To evaluate our method, we propose two new benchmarks, ToneBank and DebateMix, targeting compositional behavioral control. Empirical results across 3 model families, validated by both activation-based classifiers and LLM-based judges, demonstrate that K-Steering outperforms strong baselines in accurately steering multiple behaviors.

papers.title: What Can We Actually Steer? A Multi-Behavior Study of Activation Control
papers.research_question: How does activation steering effectiveness vary across different behavior types, and can the nature of target behaviors predict steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with internal traits like personality and misalignment being more steerable than knowledge-dependent behaviors, and vector separation does not predict success.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is not a universal control method but a semantic modulator effective for abstract, internal dispositions but ineffective for knowledge-heavy roleplay or precise formatting tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Steering effectiveness bifurcates between internal traits (e.g., personality, misalignment) and external knowledge (e.g., public figures), with internal traits being more steerable.
Trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with steering coefficient strength, peaking at moderate coefficients while coherence and relevance decline monotonically.
Vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, contradicting the intuition that larger activation differences yield better control.
Larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering without coherence collapse, improving steering quality despite smaller raw activation differences.
Misalignment behaviors such as hallucination and sycophancy are highly steerable, indicating potential safety risks where adversarial actors could easily amplify harmful traits.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily used Llama 3.1 8B, and steerability may scale non-linearly with model size.
Steering was restricted to Layer 15, and different behaviors might be localized at different layers.
Reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4.1) for evaluation introduces potential biases in scoring.
future_direction: Future work should explore whether more sophisticated vector diagnostics or non-linear relationships might better predict steerability.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require precise behavior control for safe and effective deployment across diverse applications. Activation steering offers a promising approach for LLMs' behavioral control. We focus on the question of how steering effectiveness varies across different behavior types and whether the nature of target behaviors can predict steering success. We address this through empirical analysis of activation steering across 50 behaviors that span persona archetypes, personality traits, misalignment behaviors, style cues, and impersonation of public figures. We present a set of comprehensive experiments on coefficient optimization, vector properties, and data requirements to provide comprehensive guidance for the implementation of activation steering. Our analysis demonstrates that steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with different behavioral categories exhibiting distinct response patterns to intervention strength. We find that trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with a steering coefficient strength. We also show that vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, but larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering. These findings provide empirically grounded guidance for implementing activation steering and demonstrate that steering effectiveness is heavily influenced by behavior type.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Feature Extraction and Steering for Enhanced Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How to enhance the reasoning ability of LLMs without external datasets by extracting features from vanilla Chain-of-Thought and steering internal states?
papers.core_contribution: A framework that extracts reasoning features from vanilla CoT via verbal/symbolic decomposition and steers LLM activations to enhance reasoning without external datasets or retraining.
papers.conclusion: The proposed feature extraction and steering methods enhance reasoning in LLMs, and the SAE-free approach extends the benefits to models without corresponding SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based steering improves accuracy on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
SAE-free steering works without pre-trained SAEs and achieves comparable or better performance.
Steering increases reasoning length and attention to mathematical tokens.
There is an optimal steering strength; too high strength degrades performance.
The method suppresses noisy features and amplifies task-relevant reasoning features.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to mathematical reasoning datasets.
Experiments are limited to three model families (LLaMA, DeepSeek, Gemma).
future_direction: Extend to more diverse reasoning domains such as logical reasoning, scientific problem-solving, or multi-step planning.
Apply the method to more diverse LLM architectures to verify generalizability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate the ability to solve reasoning and mathematical problems using the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) technique. Expanding CoT length, as seen in models such as DeepSeek-R1, significantly enhances this reasoning for complex problems, but requires costly and high-quality long CoT data and fine-tuning. This work, inspired by the deep thinking paradigm of DeepSeek-R1, utilizes a steering technique to enhance the reasoning ability of an LLM without external datasets. Our method first employs Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract interpretable features from vanilla CoT. These features are then used to steer the LLM's internal states during generation. Recognizing that many LLMs do not have corresponding pre-trained SAEs, we further introduce a novel SAE-free steering algorithm, which directly computes steering directions from the residual activations of an LLM, obviating the need for an explicit SAE. Experimental results demonstrate that both our SAE-based and subsequent SAE-free steering algorithms significantly enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 1, Learning Hierarchical Language Structures
papers.research_question: How do language models perform deep reasoning over hierarchical structures, and can we understand their inner workings using synthetic context-free grammars (CFGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers can learn complex context-free grammars and that their hidden states linearly encode non-terminal information, while attention patterns mimic dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn complex hierarchical structures defined by CFGs, and their internal representations and attention patterns align with dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers (GPT variants) can accurately learn and generate strings from synthetic CFGs that require dynamic programming to parse.
Hidden states of the trained transformers linearly encode non-terminal ancestor information almost perfectly.
Attention patterns in the trained models resemble the information flow of dynamic programming, with boundary-based attention.
Relative and rotary positional embeddings are crucial for learning harder CFGs, outperforming absolute positional embeddings.
Training with perturbed data (10% noise) improves robustness to corrupted prefixes.
papers.limitation: The chosen CFGs are synthetic and may not encompass all CFGs; the results are specific to the designed CFG families.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models are effective but complex, and understanding their inner workings and reasoning mechanisms is a significant challenge. Previous research has primarily explored how these models handle simple tasks like name copying or selection, and we extend this by investigating how these models perform recursive language structure reasoning defined by context-free grammars (CFGs). We introduce a family of synthetic CFGs that produce hierarchical rules, capable of generating lengthy sentences (e.g., hundreds of tokens) that are locally ambiguous and require dynamic programming to parse. Despite this complexity, we demonstrate that generative models like GPT can accurately learn and reason over CFG-defined hierarchies and generate sentences based on it. We explore the model's internals, revealing that its hidden states precisely capture the structure of CFGs, and its attention patterns resemble the information passing in a dynamic programming algorithm. This paper also presents several corollaries, including showing why absolute positional embeddings is inferior to relative and rotary embeddings; uniform attention alone is surprisingly effective (motivating our follow-up work on Canon layers); encoder-only models (e.g., BERT, DeBERTa) struggle with deep structure reasoning on CFGs compared to autoregressive models (e.g., GPT); and injecting structural or syntactic noise into pretraining data markedly improves robustness to corrupted language prompts.

papers.title: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space
papers.research_question: How can we control specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Angular Steering, a rotation-based framework for fine-grained behavior control in LLMs that generalizes existing activation steering methods and maintains general language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: Angular Steering offers a principled, flexible, and robust framework for behavior control in LLMs, enabling fine-grained modulation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors like refusal and compliance by rotating activations in a fixed 2D subspace.
The method generalizes existing activation addition and directional ablation techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework.
Angular Steering maintains general language modeling performance (e.g., on TINYBENCHMARKS) while effectively steering behavior.
Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant, improves robustness and coherence by rotating only activations aligned with the target feature.
Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show the method's flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches.
papers.limitation: The method requires a contrastive dataset to extract the feature direction, which may not always be available.
future_direction: Extending Angular Steering to multi-feature steering and dynamic plane selection.
papers.abstract: Controlling specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities is a central challenge for safe and reliable artificial intelligence deployment. Current steering methods, such as vector addition and directional ablation, are constrained within a two-dimensional subspace defined by the activation and feature direction, making them sensitive to chosen parameters and potentially affecting unrelated features due to unintended interactions in activation space. We introduce Angular Steering, a novel and flexible method for behavior modulation that operates by rotating activations within a fixed two-dimensional subspace. By formulating steering as a geometric rotation toward or away from a target behavior direction, Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors such as refusal and compliance. We demonstrate this method using refusal steering emotion steering as use cases. Additionally, we propose Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant that rotates only activations aligned with the target feature, further enhancing stability and coherence. Angular Steering generalizes existing addition and orthogonalization techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework, simplifying parameter selection and maintaining model stability across a broader range of adjustments. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show that Angular Steering achieves robust behavioral control while maintaining general language modeling performance, underscoring its flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/lone17/angular-steering/.

papers.title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models
papers.research_question: Can editing representations, instead of weights, be a more powerful alternative for parameter-efficient finetuning of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representation Finetuning (ReFT), a family of parameter-efficient finetuning methods that edit hidden representations instead of weights, and shows that it is more parameter-efficient and often outperforms existing PEFTs.
papers.conclusion: ReFT methods are a promising alternative to weight-based PEFTs, offering a better balance of efficiency and performance, and are worthy of further exploration.
papers.key_findings:
ReFT methods are 15×–65× more parameter-efficient than LoRA.
LoReFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on commonsense reasoning, instruction-following, and natural language understanding.
ReFT methods are less effective on arithmetic reasoning tasks, possibly due to the length of chain-of-thought generations.
ReFT performance scales with model size.
LoReFT outperforms full finetuning on instruction-following with only 0.0039% of parameters.
papers.limitation: ReFTs may have trouble with chain-of-thought reasoning tasks due to the length of generations and overall greater difficulty of the task.
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods seek to adapt large neural models via updates to a small number of weights. However, much prior interpretability work has shown that representations encode rich semantic information, suggesting that editing representations might be a more powerful alternative. We pursue this hypothesis by developing a family of Representation Finetuning (ReFT) methods. ReFT methods operate on a frozen base model and learn task-specific interventions on hidden representations. We define a strong instance of the ReFT family, Low-rank Linear Subspace ReFT (LoReFT), and we identify an ablation of this method that trades some performance for increased efficiency. Both are drop-in replacements for existing PEFTs and learn interventions that are 15x--65x more parameter-efficient than LoRA. We showcase LoReFT on eight commonsense reasoning tasks, four arithmetic reasoning tasks, instruction-tuning, and GLUE. In all these evaluations, our ReFTs deliver the best balance of efficiency and performance, and almost always outperform state-of-the-art PEFTs. We release a generic ReFT training library publicly at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyreft.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Review of: "Improving Instruction-Following in Language Models through Activation Steering"
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be used to enhance instruction-following in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes activation steering to improve instruction-following in language models, demonstrating enhanced adherence to constraints on IFEval benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering enhances model adherence to various constraints in instruction-following tasks.
The method shows limited improvement in more capable models like Gemma 9B compared to Gemma 2B.

papers.title: Dialz: A Python Toolkit for Steering Vectors
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dialz, a Python toolkit for creating contrastive pair datasets, computing and applying steering vectors, and visualizing their effects, facilitating research into model safety and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Dialz provides a robust foundation for steering vector research, empowering researchers to probe, control, and improve the behavior of large language models for more transparent and reliable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors constructed with Dialz can effectively reduce stereotypical outputs in language models, outperforming simple prompting interventions.
The toolkit's visualization module can highlight which tokens in an input align with a given steering vector, aiding interpretability.
Dialz provides a modular and user-friendly framework for rapid experimentation with steering vectors on open-source LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Effectiveness of steering vectors is highly dependent on the quality and balance of the contrastive datasets used to compute them.
Evaluation primarily relies on LLM-as-a-judge metrics (e.g., GPT-4o ratings), which may be biased and may not reflect human judgment.
Visualization tools are qualitative and require manual inspection to extract insights.
Tested on a limited set of models (e.g., Mistral 7B, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct), and generalizability to larger or different architectures is not evaluated.
future_direction: Incorporating the use of Sparse Autoencoders to enhance interpretability.
Incorporating a wider range of datasets, including those covering additional safety domains.
Systematic studies on how steering vectors influence model accuracy across various downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: We introduce Dialz, a framework for advancing research on steering vectors for open-source LLMs, implemented in Python. Steering vectors allow users to modify activations at inference time to amplify or weaken a 'concept', e.g. honesty or positivity, providing a more powerful alternative to prompting or fine-tuning. Dialz supports a diverse set of tasks, including creating contrastive pair datasets, computing and applying steering vectors, and visualizations. Unlike existing libraries, Dialz emphasizes modularity and usability, enabling both rapid prototyping and in-depth analysis. We demonstrate how Dialz can be used to reduce harmful outputs such as stereotypes, while also providing insights into model behaviour across different layers. We release Dialz with full documentation, tutorials, and support for popular open-source models to encourage further research in safe and controllable language generation. Dialz enables faster research cycles and facilitates insights into model interpretability, paving the way for safer, more transparent, and more reliable AI systems.

papers.title: Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made adaptive so that interventions are applied only when necessary, decoupling when to steer from how to steer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering (DSAS), a method-agnostic framework that adaptively modulates the strength of existing steering methods across layers and inputs, improving the trade-off between desired behavior (e.g., toxicity reduction) and model utility.
papers.conclusion: DSAS is an effective, general framework for conditional activation steering that decouples when to steer from how to steer, consistently improving the trade-off between behavior modification (e.g., toxicity mitigation) and model performance preservation across modalities.
papers.key_findings:
DSAS consistently improves the Pareto front for toxicity mitigation versus capability retention across different steering methods (CAA, ITI, LinEAS) and models (Qwen 2.5, Gemma 2).
DSAS can be trained end-to-end (E2E-DSAS) and matches or outperforms the vanilla DSAS.
DSAS works across modalities (text and image) without modification, enabling concept-specific modulation in text-to-image generation.
DSAS introduces minimal computational overhead and improves interpretability by pinpointing which tokens require steering and by how much.
DSAS outperforms recent conditional steering methods such as CAST and MERA in toxicity mitigation with higher performance retention.
