The identifiability guarantees rely on assumptions such as the Linear Representation Hypothesis and sufficient diversity of multi-concept shifts, which may not hold in all practical settings.
The theoretical analysis assumes the encoder dimension is known (equal to the number of varying concepts |V|), but in practice this is often unknown and a larger dimension is used, which can affect identifiability.
future_direction: Extending the method to non-linear representations.
Applying the approach to other modalities beyond text.
Scaling the method to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: Steering methods manipulate the representations of large language models (LLMs) to induce responses that have desired properties, e.g., truthfulness, offering a promising approach for LLM alignment without the need for fine-tuning. Traditionally, steering has relied on supervision, such as from contrastive pairs of prompts that vary in a single target concept, which is costly to obtain and limits the speed of steering research. An appealing alternative is to use unsupervised approaches such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to map LLM embeddings to sparse representations that capture human-interpretable concepts. However, without further assumptions, SAEs may not be identifiable: they could learn latent dimensions that entangle multiple concepts, leading to unintentional steering of unrelated properties. We introduce Sparse Shift Autoencoders (SSAEs) that instead map the differences between embeddings to sparse representations. Crucially, we show that SSAEs are identifiable from paired observations that vary in \textit{multiple unknown concepts}, leading to accurate steering of single concepts without the need for supervision. We empirically demonstrate accurate steering across semi-synthetic and real-world language datasets using Llama-3.1 embeddings.

papers.title: Spherical Steering: Geometry-Aware Activation Rotation for Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we achieve effective inference-time control of language models without degrading their open-ended generation capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Spherical Steering, a training-free activation rotation method that improves multiple-choice accuracy and open-ended generation quality by preserving activation norms and using geometry-aware rotations.
papers.conclusion: Spherical Steering, a training-free activation steering method using geodesic rotation, consistently improves accuracy while enhancing open-ended generation quality, highlighting activation rotation as an effective primitive for inference-time control.
papers.key_findings:
Spherical Steering outperforms additive baselines (e.g., ITI, CAA) on multiple-choice benchmarks, improving average accuracy by over 8 points.
The method maintains or improves open-ended generation quality (TRUE×INFO) while boosting accuracy, unlike additive methods which degrade generation.
Norm-preserving rotation is more collapse-efficient than additive steering, achieving greater performance gains per unit of representational change.
The method is compatible with in-context learning, providing additional gains when combined with few-shot prompting.
The vMF confidence gate enables input-adaptive steering, improving selectivity and controllability.
future_direction: principled multi-layer layer selection
layer-adaptive calibration
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering has emerged as a promising paradigm for controlling language models (LMs) without the cost of retraining. However, standard approaches typically rely on activation addition, a geometric operation that inevitably alters the magnitude of hidden representations. This raises concerns about representation collapse and degradation of open-ended generation capabilities. In this work, we explore Spherical Steering, a training-free primitive that resolves this trade-off through activation rotation. Rather than shifting activations with a fixed vector, our method rotates them along a geodesic toward a target direction, guiding the activation toward the target concept while preserving the integrity of the signal. To further enhance adaptivity, we incorporate a confidence gate that dynamically modulates steering strength based on input uncertainty. Extensive experiments across multiple-choice benchmarks demonstrate that Spherical Steering significantly outperforms addition-based baselines (notably by +10% on TruthfulQA, COPA, and Storycloze), while simultaneously maintaining the model's general open-ended generation quality. This work highlights the value of geometric consistency, suggesting that norm-preserving rotation is a robust and effective primitive for precise inference-time control.

papers.title: CorrSteer: Generation-Time LLM Steering via Correlated Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we effectively steer large language models using Sparse Autoencoder features without requiring contrastive datasets or large activation storage?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CorrSteer, a fully automated pipeline that selects task-relevant Sparse Autoencoder features by correlating generation-time activations with task outcomes, and uses these features to steer model behavior with reduced side effects.
papers.conclusion: CorrSteer establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across diverse language model applications.
papers.key_findings:
CorrSteer improves performance on QA, bias mitigation, and safety benchmarks, e.g., +3.3% on MMLU and +27.2% on HarmBench.
Correlation-based feature selection is effective and scalable, requiring only inference-time activations and no contrastive data.
Multi-layer steering (CorrSteer-A, CorrSteer-P) outperforms single-feature steering, suggesting collaborative circuit effects.
CorrSteer reduces side effects compared to fine-tuning, as measured by the Side Effect Ratio (SER).
Selected features are semantically interpretable and align with task requirements (e.g., refusal features for safety, structured output for multiple-choice).
papers.limitation:
CorrSteer is static and cannot easily adapt to dynamic tasks or separate benign from harmful requests without additional context.
The method may capture spurious correlations rather than causal relationships, especially with limited samples.
future_direction: Extend CorrSteer to dynamic tasks and sequential decision-making.
Improve feature selection to further reduce spurious correlations.
Apply the method to larger models and more complex domains.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable features from large language models (LLMs) without supervision. However, their effectiveness in downstream steering tasks is limited by the requirement for contrastive datasets or large activation storage. To address these limitations, we propose CorrSteer, which selects features by correlating sample correctness with SAE activations from generated tokens at inference time. This approach uses only inference-time activations to extract more relevant features, thereby reducing spurious correlations. It also obtains steering coefficients from average activations, automating the entire pipeline. Our method shows improved task performance on QA, bias mitigation, jailbreaking prevention, and reasoning benchmarks on Gemma-2 2B and LLaMA-3.1 8B, notably achieving a +3.3% improvement in MMLU performance with 4000 samples and a +27.2% improvement in HarmBench with only 108 samples. Selected features demonstrate semantically meaningful patterns aligned with each task's requirements, revealing the underlying capabilities that drive performance. Our work establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across language model applications.

papers.title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed
papers.research_question: Can activation steering suppress evaluation-awareness in LLMs and make them act as if deployed during evaluation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that adding a steering vector to an LLM's activations can suppress evaluation-awareness and make the model act like it is deployed during evaluation, validated by training an evaluation-aware model organism.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering can be used to make models act as if deployed during evaluation, which can improve the reliability of safety evaluations by mitigating evaluation-awareness.
papers.key_findings:
Successfully trained an evaluation-aware model organism that writes Python type hints in evaluation contexts but not in deployment contexts.
Activation steering can suppress evaluation-awareness and elicit deployment behavior even when the evaluation cue (Wood Labs) is present and simple deployment prompts fail.
The steering vector, extracted from the pre-fine-tuned model, remains effective after fine-tuning, suggesting it does not directly encode the target behavior.
Steering changes the model's explicit beliefs about its deployment status, as reflected in its chain-of-thought reasoning.
The method works throughout multiple rounds of expert iteration, maintaining a gap between evaluation and deployment behavior.
papers.limitation: The work did not explore contexts where the model organism would need to determine whether it is being evaluated using subtle contextual clues other than the explicit Wood Labs cue.
future_direction: Explore other model editing methods for mitigating evaluation awareness.
Apply activation steering to critical evaluations such as dangerous capabilities evaluations or honeypot evaluations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes detect when they are being evaluated and adjust their behavior to appear more aligned, compromising the reliability of safety evaluations. In this paper, we show that adding a steering vector to an LLM's activations can suppress evaluation-awareness and make the model act like it is deployed during evaluation. To study our steering technique, we train an LLM to exhibit evaluation-aware behavior using a two-step training process designed to mimic how this behavior could emerge naturally. First, we perform continued pretraining on documents with factual descriptions of the model (1) using Python type hints during evaluation but not during deployment and (2) recognizing that the presence of a certain evaluation cue always means that it is being tested. Then, we train the model with expert iteration to use Python type hints in evaluation settings. The resulting model is evaluation-aware: it writes type hints in evaluation contexts more than deployment contexts. We find that activation steering can suppress evaluation awareness and make the model act like it is deployed even when the cue is present. Importantly, we constructed our steering vector using the original model before our additional training. Our results suggest that AI evaluators could improve the reliability of safety evaluations by steering models to act like they are deployed.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Chain-of-Thought Compression
papers.research_question: Can we compress chains of thought without retraining, by manipulating the model’s hidden representations at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Activation-Steered Compression (ASC), a training-free inference-time method that compresses chains of thought by steering residual stream activations, with a theoretical framework for safe steering via KL-divergence bounds.
papers.conclusion: ASC is a training-free method that compresses CoTs via activation steering, demonstrating that conciseness is steerable through the model's internal geometry, advancing efficient LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
ASC reduces CoT length by up to 67.43% on MATH500 and GSM8K without accuracy degradation.
ASC delivers an average 2.73x inference speedup on an 8B model.
Steering vectors extracted from different datasets show strong alignment (cosine similarity 0.92), indicating verbosity reduction is a shared latent direction.
The KL-constrained scaling method selects a steering strength that aligns with the empirical breakpoint where performance begins to degrade.
ASC is orthogonal to existing compression methods and requires no retraining.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at complex reasoning when they include intermediate steps, known as "chains of thought" (CoTs). However, these rationales are often overly verbose, even for simple problems, leading to wasted context, increased latency, and higher energy consumption. We observe that verbose, English-heavy CoTs and concise, math-centric CoTs occupy distinct regions in the model's residual-stream activation space. By extracting and injecting a "steering vector" to transition between these modes, we can reliably shift generation toward more concise reasoning, effectively compressing CoTs without retraining. We formalize this approach as Activation-Steered Compression (ASC), an inference-time technique that shortens reasoning traces by directly modifying hidden representations. In addition, we provide a theoretical analysis of the impact of ASC on the output distribution, derived from a closed-form KL-divergence-bounded constraint to regulate steering strength. Using only 100 paired verbose and concise examples, ASC achieves up to 67.43% reduction in CoT length on MATH500 and GSM8K datasets, while maintaining accuracy across 7B, 8B, and 32B parameter models. As a training-free method, ASC introduces negligible runtime overhead and, on MATH500, delivers an average 2.73x speedup in end-to-end reasoning wall-clock time on an 8B model. This makes ASC a practical and efficient tool for streamlining the deployment of reasoning-capable LLMs in latency- or cost-sensitive settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/ArminAzizi98/ASC

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Steering LLMs for Formal Theorem Proving
papers.research_question: How does informal natural language context influence internal reasoning in LLMs for theorem proving, and can activation steering improve proof generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an activation steering method that extracts linear directions from residual activations associated with informal reasoning and uses them to guide proof synthesis, improving performance without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering enhances LLMs' theorem-proving capabilities without fine-tuning and provides insights into how informal language is represented in activation space.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering improves theorem-proving performance across models and benchmarks.
Steering vectors are most effective when applied to later layers.
Steering improves proof search efficiency and can lead to shorter proofs.
Steering vectors generalize across different proof assistants (Lean and Coq).
Steering is parameter-efficient and competitive with LoRA fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The study does not systematically evaluate the relevance or factual correctness of the natural language inputs.
Steering can introduce failure cases due to biases in the data used to construct the vectors.
future_direction: Analyze the relationship between instruction quality and proof validity.
Characterize the inductive biases embedded in steering vectors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in automated theorem proving use Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate informal mathematical statements into formal proofs. However, informal cues are often ambiguous or lack strict logical structure, making it hard for models to interpret them precisely. While existing methods achieve strong performance, little is known about how LLMs internally represent informal cues, or how these influence proof generation. To address this, we explore \textit{activation steering}, an inference-time intervention that identifies linear directions in residual activations associated with informal reasoning traces and adjusts them to improve proof construction without fine-tuning. This mechanism also yields interpretable information about how reasoning is internally encoded in the activation space of LLMs. We test our method for generating formal proofs from already-formalized theorems. Our contributions are twofold: (1) a novel activation-based intervention for guiding proof synthesis in LLMs; and (2) demonstration that this intervention improves performance under two decoding strategies (sampling and best-first search) without any further training.

papers.title: Constrained belief updates explain geometric structures in transformer representations
papers.research_question: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? How do transformers resolve the conflict between optimal Bayesian belief updating (a recursive process) and their parallelized, attention-driven architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating—a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. It explains why specific intermediate geometric structures emerge in transformer representations.
papers.conclusion: The geometric structures in transformer representations are a mathematical signature of how architectural constraints warp optimal Bayesian inference, revealing a precise interplay between theoretical necessity and implementation.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating due to architectural constraints, bending optimal Bayesian inference into attention's parallelizable form.
The attention mechanism in the first layer implements a spectral algorithm that builds constrained beliefs, with attention weights approximating the decay of influence via eigenvalues of the data-generating transition matrix.
Intermediate representations (after attention) are fractals matching the constrained belief geometry, while final representations (after MLP) match the full, unconstrained belief geometry.
The attention pattern, OV vectors, and token embeddings can be theoretically predicted from the constrained belief updating equations.
For negative eigenvalues in the transition matrix (oscillatory dynamics), multiple attention heads are required to capture the full update pattern due to the non-negativity constraint of attention.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is conducted on a tractable family of hidden Markov models (Mess3), which is a simplified setting.
As the HMM parameter α moves away from a central range, deviations between predicted and actual representations increase, and a complete characterization of these deviations remains for future work.
future_direction: A complete characterization of how deviations between predicted and actual representations scale with the HMM parameter α.
Applying the methodology to more complex cases, such as large language models trained on natural text, where the same tension between architecture and optimal inference is anticipated.
papers.abstract: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? In this work, we provide evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating -- a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. We integrate the model-agnostic theory of optimal prediction with mechanistic interpretability to analyze transformers trained on a tractable family of hidden Markov models that generate rich geometric patterns in neural activations. Our primary analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, revealing how the first attention layer implements these constrained updates, with extensions to multi-layer architectures demonstrating how subsequent layers refine these representations. We find that attention carries out an algorithm with a natural interpretation in the probability simplex, and create representations with distinctive geometric structure. We show how both the algorithmic behavior and the underlying geometry of these representations can be theoretically predicted in detail -- including the attention pattern, OV-vectors, and embedding vectors -- by modifying the equations for optimal future token predictions to account for the architectural constraints of attention. Our approach provides a principled lens on how architectural constraints shape the implementation of optimal prediction, revealing why transformers develop specific intermediate geometric structures.

papers.title: Unveiling Transformers with LEGO: a synthetic reasoning task
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures learn to follow a chain of reasoning, and how do architectural choices (like weight tying) and data composition (like pretraining) affect their generalization and the emergence of specific attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the LEGO synthetic reasoning task to study how Transformers learn to follow chains of reasoning. It identifies that successful models develop specialized attention heads for association (long-range identity matching) and manipulation (short-range operations), and based on this insight, proposes the LEGO attention module which reduces FLOPs while maintaining or improving performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The LEGO task provides a controlled setting to understand how Transformers learn reasoning, revealing the importance of structured attention patterns for generalization. These insights can guide architectural design, as demonstrated by the proposed LEGO attention module which offers efficiency gains.
papers.key_findings:
Classical generalization can be deceptive, as models can learn 'shortcut' solutions that do not follow the intended chain of reasoning and impede out-of-distribution generalization.
Iterative architectures like ALBERT, which share weights across layers, exhibit better length extrapolation (generalization to longer reasoning chains) than non-iterative architectures like BERT, suggesting an inductive bias towards implementing a 'for-loop'.
Pretraining helps generalization on the LEGO task primarily by providing a beneficial initialization with structured attention patterns (association and manipulation heads), rather than by encoding complex task-specific knowledge.
Models can be incentivized to learn more robust, iterative solutions through techniques like stochastic depth training, which improves length extrapolation.
The identified structured attention patterns motivate a new LEGO attention module, which when used as a drop-in replacement for standard attention, reduces computational cost and matches or improves performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic task, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Applying the insights from the LEGO task to currently challenging mathematical reasoning tasks like MATH and IsarStep.
Exploring the application of the LEGO attention module to other domains and tasks.
papers.abstract: We propose a synthetic reasoning task, LEGO (Learning Equality and Group Operations), that encapsulates the problem of following a chain of reasoning, and we study how the Transformer architectures learn this task. We pay special attention to data effects such as pretraining (on seemingly unrelated NLP tasks) and dataset composition (e.g., differing chain length at training and test time), as well as architectural variants such as weight-tied layers or adding convolutional components. We study how the trained models eventually succeed at the task, and in particular, we manage to understand some of the attention heads as well as how the information flows in the network. In particular, we have identified a novel \emph{association} pattern that globally attends only to identical tokens. Based on these observations we propose a hypothesis that here pretraining helps for LEGO tasks due to certain structured attention patterns, and we experimentally verify this hypothesis. We also observe that in some data regime the trained transformer finds ``shortcut" solutions to follow the chain of reasoning, which impedes the model's robustness, and moreover we propose ways to prevent it. Motivated by our findings on structured attention patterns, we propose the LEGO attention module, a drop-in replacement for vanilla attention heads. This architectural change significantly reduces Flops and maintains or even \emph{improves} the model's performance at large-scale pretraining.

papers.title: Hallucination reduction with CASAL: Contrastive Activation Steering For Amortized Learning
papers.research_question: How can we reduce hallucinations in LLMs by amortizing activation steering into model weights, enabling models to abstain from unknown questions without inference-time intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CASAL, an efficient method that amortizes activation steering into model weights, enabling LLMs to answer known questions and abstain from unknown ones by training only a submodule of a single transformer layer.
papers.conclusion: CASAL is an effective, efficient, and generalizable method for reducing hallucinations by amortizing activation steering into model weights, representing a promising step for practical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
CASAL reduces hallucination rates by 30-40% across multiple short-form QA benchmarks.
CASAL is ~30x more compute-efficient and ~20x more data-efficient than LoRA-based baselines like SFT and DPO.
CASAL generalizes effectively to out-of-distribution domains and across different data groups.
CASAL works for both text-only and vision-language models, and for both dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models.
CASAL reduces hallucinations without degrading general capabilities or causing excessive refusals on known queries.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities but often hallucinate, confidently providing incorrect answers instead of admitting ignorance. Prior work has shown that models encode linear representations of their own knowledge and that activation steering can reduce hallucinations. These approaches, however, require real-time monitoring and intervention during inference. We introduce Contrastive Activation Steering for Amortized Learning (CASAL), an efficient algorithm that connects interpretability with amortized optimization. CASAL directly bakes the benefits of activation steering into model's weights. Once trained, LLMs answer questions they know while abstaining from answering those they do not. CASAL's light-weight design requires training only a submodule of a single transformer layer and yet reduces hallucination by 30%-40% across multiple short-form QA benchmarks. CASAL is 30x more compute-efficient and 20x more data-efficient than strong LoRA-based baselines such as SFT and DPO, boosting its practical applicability in data scarce domains. Importantly, CASAL also generalizes effectively to out-of-distribution (OOD) domains. We showcase CASAL's flexibility in mitigating hallucinations in both text-only and vision-language models. To our knowledge, CASAL is the first steering-based training method that has been shown to be effective for both dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. CASAL represents a promising step forward for applying interpretability-inspired method for practical deployment in production systems.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive large language models internally represent and process emotional information to infer emotions from text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that emotion representations in LLMs are functionally localized to mid-layers and that causal interventions on appraisal concepts can steer emotion inference in psychologically plausible ways.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a mechanistic understanding of emotion inference in LLMs and demonstrates causal intervention methods to control emotion inference, with potential applications in safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion representations are functionally localized to specific mid-layers across diverse model families and sizes.
Activation patching reveals that MHSA and FFN units in mid-layers are critical for emotion inference.
Attention patterns in mid-layers shift to emotionally loaded tokens.
Appraisal concepts are linearly represented in the model and their modulation can steer emotion inference.
The structure of emotion representations aligns with cognitive appraisal theory from psychology.
papers.limitation: Focusing only on correctly classified examples may introduce bias toward unambiguous emotional content.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promising capabilities in predicting human emotions from text. However, the mechanisms through which these models process emotional stimuli remain largely unexplored. Our study addresses this gap by investigating how autoregressive LLMs infer emotions, showing that emotion representations are functionally localized to specific regions in the model. Our evaluation includes diverse model families and sizes and is supported by robustness checks. We then show that the identified representations are psychologically plausible by drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, a well-established psychological framework positing that emotions emerge from evaluations (appraisals) of environmental stimuli. By causally intervening on construed appraisal concepts, we steer the generation and show that the outputs align with theoretical and intuitive expectations. This work highlights a novel way to causally intervene and precisely shape emotional text generation, potentially benefiting safety and alignment in sensitive affective domains.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether masked diffusion language models admit a single activation direction for inference-time control of safety-related behaviors, and how the diffusion architecture affects the accessibility and transferability of such representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation steering for masked diffusion language models, showing that refusal behavior is governed by a consistent low-dimensional activation subspace, and that steering can effectively control safety refusal with diffusion-specific properties such as accessibility from pre-instruction tokens.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that activation steering is an effective inference-time control method for MDLMs, with diffusion-specific accessibility and localization properties, and that safety representations are architecture-dependent.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal behavior in MDLMs is governed by a single low-dimensional activation direction, enabling large and consistent shifts in refusal behavior when applied globally during reverse diffusion.
Effective refusal directions in MDLMs can be extracted from pre-instruction tokens, unlike autoregressive models, due to non-causal parallel processing.
Activation steering is most effective during early denoising steps and in mid-to-late transformer layers, with the first diffusion block contributing disproportionately.
Refusal directions transfer robustly between English and Chinese within the same MDLM, but do not reliably transfer to an autoregressive model, indicating architecture-dependent safety representations.
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text through an iterative denoising process. They have recently gained attention due to mask-parallel decoding and competitive performance with autoregressive large language models. However, effective mechanisms for inference-time control and steering in MDLMs remain largely unexplored. We present an activation-steering framework for MDLMs that computes layer-wise steering vectors from a single forward pass using contrastive examples, without simulating the denoising trajectory. These directions are applied at every reverse-diffusion step, yielding an efficient inference-time control mechanism. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct demonstrate reliable modulation of high-level attributes, with ablations examining the effects of steering across transformer sub-modules and token scope (prompt vs.\ response).

papers.title: Semantic Composition in Visually Grounded Language Models
papers.research_question: This thesis explores whether and how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces multiple methods (WinogroundVQA, Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, Causal Tracing, Syntactic MeanPool, Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization) to probe, analyze, and improve the compositional abilities of visually grounded language models.
papers.conclusion: The work explores the compositionality of visually grounded semantics, introducing methods to probe and improve it, and draws connections to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.
papers.key_findings:
Generative vision-language models like BLIP 2.0 and MiniGPT-4 perform poorly on the compositional WinogroundVQA benchmark.
Syntactic Neural Module Distillation reveals that larger sentence embedding models (GTR-T5) are more compositional, but model size is not the only determining factor.
Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization (CACR) improves relation alignment in vision-language models and outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method (IAIS) on the Winoground benchmark.
papers.limitation:
Due to compute restrictions, hyperparameter tuning for the SynNaMoN experiments was unfeasible, and the dataset had to be constrained to a subset of trees and production rules.
The choice of linguistic formalism (Penn Treebank) may influence the probing results of compositional structure.
future_direction: Exploring whether different linguistic formalisms are better proxies for a model's compositional structure.
Further work on the causal tracing experiment for image captioning models (implementation in progress).
papers.abstract: What is sentence meaning and its ideal representation? Much of the expressive power of human language derives from semantic composition, the mind's ability to represent meaning hierarchically & relationally over constituents. At the same time, much sentential meaning is outside the text and requires grounding in sensory, motor, and experiential modalities to be adequately learned. Although large language models display considerable compositional ability, recent work shows that visually-grounded language models drastically fail to represent compositional structure. In this thesis, we explore whether & how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so. Specifically, we introduce 1) WinogroundVQA, a new compositional visual question answering benchmark, 2) Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, a measure of compositional ability in sentence embedding models, 3) Causal Tracing for Image Captioning Models to locate neural representations vital for vision-language composition, 4) Syntactic MeanPool to inject a compositional inductive bias into sentence embeddings, and 5) Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization, a self-supervised objective function for vision-language relation alignment. We close by discussing connections of our work to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.

papers.title: SteerX: Disentangled Steering for LLM Personalization
papers.research_question: How can we improve activation steering for LLM personalization by disentangling preference-driven components from user data, focusing only on the parts that truly reflect user preferences?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SteerX, a disentangled steering method that uses causal inference to identify preference-driven tokens in user history and transforms them into a coherent style description, leading to more accurate activation steering vectors for LLM personalization.
papers.conclusion: SteerX effectively enhances activation steering for LLM personalization by focusing on preference-driven components, leading to improved personalized text generation across tasks and model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
SteerX improves personalization performance over existing steering methods (CAS and COS) across multiple metrics and LLM sizes (8B and 14B).
The disentangling step (identifying personalized tokens) and the smoothing step (transforming tokens into a coherent description) both contribute to the performance gains.
The method demonstrates broad applicability by enhancing different steering backbones (influence vector and style vector).
Token-level causal effect analysis reveals a long-tailed distribution, with a subset of high-influence tokens corresponding to preference-driven components.
The smoothing step that generates a coherent style description from discrete tokens provides a stronger and more stable steering signal.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable success in recent years, enabling a wide range of applications, including intelligent assistants that support users' daily life and work. A critical factor in building such assistants is personalizing LLMs, as user preferences and needs vary widely. Activation steering, which directly leverages directions representing user preference in the LLM activation space to adjust its behavior, offers a cost-effective way to align the model's outputs with individual users. However, existing methods rely on all historical data to compute the steering vector, ignoring that not all content reflects true user preferences, which undermines the personalization signal. To address this, we propose SteerX, a disentangled steering method that isolates preference-driven components from preference-agnostic components. Grounded in causal inference theory, SteerX estimates token-level causal effects to identify preference-driven tokens, transforms these discrete signals into a coherent description, and then leverages them to steer personalized LLM generation. By focusing on the truly preference-driven information, SteerX produces more accurate activation steering vectors and enhances personalization. Experiments on two representative steering backbone methods across real-world datasets demonstrate that SteerX consistently enhances steering vector quality, offering a practical solution for more effective LLM personalization.

papers.title: Task Vectors, Learned Not Extracted: Performance Gains and Mechanistic Insight
papers.research_question: How can we obtain effective task vectors for in-context learning, and what are the mechanisms by which they influence model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Learned Task Vectors (LTVs), which are directly trained and outperform extracted task vectors, and provides a mechanistic analysis showing that task vectors primarily act through attention-head OV circuits and propagate linearly through subsequent layers.
papers.conclusion: LTVs provide an efficient and flexible method for obtaining effective task vectors and offer a principled lens into the mechanistic foundations of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
LTVs consistently outperform extracted task vectors (Vanilla TV and Function Vector) and match or exceed in-context learning performance across multiple models and tasks.
LTVs are flexible and can be effectively injected at arbitrary layers, token positions, and even into in-context learning prompts.
The low-level mechanism of task vectors involves interaction with attention-head OV circuits, with a small subset of 'key heads' being most decisive.
Despite Transformer nonlinearities, the propagation of injected task vectors through subsequent layers is largely linear, characterized by rotation toward task-relevant subspaces in early layers and scaling in magnitude in later layers.
Task vectors exhibit compositionality and cross-task generalization that is constrained by overlap in the label space of tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can perform new tasks from in-context demonstrations, a phenomenon known as in-context learning (ICL). Recent work suggests that these demonstrations are compressed into task vectors (TVs), compact task representations that LLMs exploit for predictions. However, prior studies typically extract TVs from model outputs or hidden states using cumbersome and opaque methods, and they rarely elucidate the mechanisms by which TVs influence computation. In this work, we address both limitations. First, we propose directly training Learned Task Vectors (LTVs), which surpass extracted TVs in accuracy and exhibit superior flexibility-acting effectively at arbitrary layers, positions, and even with ICL prompts. Second, through systematic analysis, we investigate the mechanistic role of TVs, showing that at the low level they steer predictions primarily through attention-head OV circuits, with a small subset of "key heads" most decisive. At a higher level, we find that despite Transformer nonlinearities, TV propagation is largely linear: early TVs are rotated toward task-relevant subspaces to improve logits of relevant labels, while later TVs are predominantly scaled in magnitude. Taken together, LTVs not only provide a practical approach for obtaining effective TVs but also offer a principled lens into the mechanistic foundations of ICL.

papers.title: Beyond Prompt Engineering: Robust Behavior Control in LLMs via Steering Target Atoms
papers.research_question: How can we achieve precise control over language model generation by isolating and manipulating disentangled knowledge components (target atoms) using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Steering Target Atoms (STA), a method that uses SAE-decoupled representations to identify and manipulate target atoms for precise behavior control in LLMs, demonstrating improved safety and robustness over prompt engineering and other steering methods.
papers.conclusion: STA provides a novel method for precise behavior control in LLMs, offering superior robustness and flexibility compared to prompt engineering, and can be extended to control reasoning in large reasoning models.
papers.key_findings:
STA achieves state-of-the-art detoxification performance on safety benchmarks, with minimal side effects on general capabilities.
Steering strategies (including STA) are more robust and flexible than prompt engineering, especially in adversarial scenarios.
Steering vectors remain effective even with very few instances (as few as 4).
Steering can control the length of chain-of-thought reasoning in large reasoning models, mitigating overthinking.
Steering in intermediate layers (layers 24-25) is more effective for behavior control.
papers.limitation:
SAE-based methods can be outperformed by simple baselines in some steering tasks, and STA shows limited effectiveness in the personality domain.
Experiments are limited to Gemma and Llama models due to limited public SAE availability.
The study focuses on safety and personality domains; applicability to other domains like multi-turn dialogue or complex reasoning is not validated.
future_direction: Extend STA to a broader range of LLMs, including larger and more diverse architectures.
Validate STA in other nuanced domains such as multi-turn dialogue or complex reasoning tasks.
Further investigate the performance divergence of SAE-based methods in different domains.
papers.abstract: Precise control over language model generation is vital for ensuring both safety and reliability. Although prompt engineering and steering are commonly used to intervene in model behaviors, the vast number of parameters in models often results in highly intertwined internal representations. This interdependency can limit control precision and sometimes lead to unintended side effects. Recent research has explored the use of sparse autoencoders (SAE) to disentangle knowledge in high-dimensional spaces for steering. However, these applications have been limited to toy tasks owing to the nontrivial issue of locating atomic knowledge components. In this paper, we propose Steering Target Atoms (STA), a novel method that isolates and manipulates disentangled knowledge components to enhance safety. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Further analysis reveals that steering exhibits superior robustness and flexibility, particularly in adversarial scenarios. We also apply the steering strategy to the large reasoning model, confirming its effectiveness in precise reasoning control.

papers.title: Patterns and Mechanisms of Contrastive Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: What are the patterns, mechanisms, and limitations of Contrastive Activation Engineering for steering LLM outputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically investigates Contrastive Activation Engineering, revealing that steering vectors are only reliable within the distribution they are computed from, have diminishing returns with sample size, can be adversarially nullified, and generally harm model perplexity, with larger models being more resistant.
papers.conclusion: CAE shows promise for controlling LLM behavior but has limitations in out-of-distribution generalization and performance degradation, necessitating careful deployment and further research.
papers.key_findings:
CAE is only reliably effective when applied to in-distribution contexts.
Increasing the number of samples used to generate steering vectors has diminishing returns at around 80 samples.
Steering vectors are susceptible to adversarial inputs that reverse the steered behavior.
Steering vectors harm the overall model perplexity.
Larger models are more resistant to steering-induced degradation.
papers.limitation:
In-distribution evaluation introduces noise from the model’s default tendency on each behavior.
Out-of-distribution evaluation relies on the assumption that LLMs can act in place of human evaluators, which was not verified.
The out-of-distribution evaluation dataset is not grounded in real user queries.
future_direction: Improving out-of-distribution robustness
Developing automated methods for balancing steering effectiveness against potential negative impacts on model performance
Expanding the set of CAE techniques and models studied
papers.abstract: Controlling the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge due to their inherent complexity and opacity. While techniques like fine-tuning can modify model behavior, they typically require extensive computational resources. Recent work has introduced a class of contrastive activation engineering (CAE) techniques as promising approaches for steering LLM outputs through targeted modifications to their internal representations. Applied at inference-time with zero cost, CAE has the potential to introduce a new paradigm of flexible, task-specific LLM behavior tuning. We analyze the performance of CAE in in-distribution, out-of-distribution settings, evaluate drawbacks, and begin to develop comprehensive guidelines for its effective deployment. We find that 1. CAE is only reliably effective when applied to in-distribution contexts. 2. Increasing the number of samples used to generate steering vectors has diminishing returns at around 80 samples. 3. Steering vectors are susceptible to adversarial inputs that reverses the behavior that is steered for. 4. Steering vectors harm the overall model perplexity. 5. Larger models are more resistant to steering-induced degradation.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Chain-of-Thought: A Latent Computational Mode in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of Chain-of-Thought prompting in triggering reasoning in large language models? Is CoT the unique mechanism or just one of several triggers for a latent reasoning capability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning in LLMs can be triggered by steering latent internal features identified via Sparse Autoencoders, indicating that Chain-of-Thought prompting is not the unique pathway but one of several triggers for an underlying reasoning mechanism.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning in large language models can be triggered by activating latent internal features, showing that Chain-of-Thought prompting is not unique and that activation-level interventions are useful for understanding and controlling reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Steering a single reasoning-related latent feature improves reasoning accuracy without explicit Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Early single-feature steering leads to more concise reasoning outputs in large models, matching or exceeding CoT performance with fewer tokens.
The identified reasoning feature is activated early in generation and is associated with entering a reasoning mode rather than predicting answer correctness.
The reasoning feature generalizes across different prompts that encourage reasoning (e.g., 'Explain how', 'Solve carefully'), not just step-by-step prompts.
Random feature steering does not produce similar improvements, confirming the specificity of the identified reasoning-related feature.
papers.limitation: The identified SAE features are not fully disentangled or isolated reasoning mechanisms; conclusions are based on behavioral and intervention-level evidence, not complete mechanistic characterization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has improved the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), but it remains unclear why it works and whether it is the unique mechanism for triggering reasoning in large language models. In this work, we study this question by directly analyzing and intervening on the internal representations of LLMs with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), identifying a small set of latent features that are causally associated with LLM reasoning behavior. Across multiple model families and reasoning benchmarks, we find that steering a single reasoning-related latent feature can substantially improve accuracy without explicit CoT prompting. For large models, latent steering achieves performance comparable to standard CoT prompting while producing more efficient outputs. We further observe that this reasoning-oriented internal state is triggered early in generation and can override prompt-level instructions that discourage explicit reasoning. Overall, our results suggest that multi-step reasoning in LLMs is supported by latent internal activations that can be externally activated, while CoT prompting is one effective, but not unique, way of activating this mechanism rather than its necessary cause.

papers.title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
papers.research_question: Do transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causal world models, and how are these models structured and used?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks develop causal world models, with interventions revealing an asymmetry (activation easier than suppression) and positional encodings affect the world model structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks form causal world models that capture maze connectivity, and these representations are used for solving.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causally relevant world models.
Interventions that activate features are more effective than those that remove them (asymmetry).
Models can reason about mazes with more simultaneously active features than seen during training, but fail when the same mazes are provided via longer input sequences.
Positional encoding schemes influence how world models are structured (e.g., Stan uses a compositional code, Terry uses single features).
SAEs are better than linear probes for isolating world models.
papers.limitation: Stan was unable to generalize to sequences containing more connections than it had seen during training, leading to failure in removal interventions.
future_direction: Future research could explore how to impose constraints on AI systems in terms of the features they acquire as a result of training.
Future work could investigate how these findings generalize to more complex environments and tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies in interpretability have explored the inner workings of transformer models trained on tasks across various domains, often discovering that these networks naturally develop highly structured representations. When such representations comprehensively reflect the task domain's structure, they are commonly referred to as "World Models" (WMs). In this work, we identify WMs in transformers trained on maze-solving tasks. By using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and analyzing attention patterns, we examine the construction of WMs and demonstrate consistency between SAE feature-based and circuit-based analyses. By subsequently intervening on isolated features to confirm their causal role, we find that it is easier to activate features than to suppress them. Furthermore, we find that models can reason about mazes involving more simultaneously active features than they encountered during training; however, when these same mazes (with greater numbers of connections) are provided to models via input tokens instead, the models fail. Finally, we demonstrate that positional encoding schemes appear to influence how World Models are structured within the model's residual stream.

papers.title: Extrapolation by Association: Length Generalization Transfer in Transformers
papers.research_question: Can generalization to longer inputs in one task transfer to another task that is only trained on short examples?
papers.core_contribution: Length generalization can be transferred across related tasks in transformers, and this transfer correlates with the reuse of attention heads between tasks.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can transfer length generalization capabilities across related tasks, and this transfer is associated with the reuse of attention heads, highlighting the compositional reuse of inductive structure across tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Length generalization transfers from auxiliary tasks to main tasks when trained jointly, enabling extrapolation to longer inputs.
The transfer effect is strongest when the auxiliary and main tasks are related and when the length ratio is between 0.5 and 2.
Pretraining on natural language improves length generalization transfer in downstream synthetic tasks.
Transfer correlates with shared internal computation, specifically the reuse of attention heads between tasks.
Training dynamics for length generalization transfer are unstable and sensitive to model initialization.
papers.limitation:
Lack of a formal theoretical framework for understanding when and why transfer occurs.
Experiments are limited to relatively simple algorithmic domains with well-defined length parameters and deterministic solution paths.
future_direction: Explore whether similar transfer effects exist for other generalization challenges such as compositional reasoning, distributional shifts, and task complexity.
Investigate transfer in more complex settings involving hierarchical reasoning, abstract problem-solving, or integration of multiple skills.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models have demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities in natural language domains, yet we lack a fine-grained understanding of how such generalization arises. In this paper, we investigate length generalization--the ability to extrapolate from shorter to longer inputs--through the lens of \textit{task association}. We find that length generalization can be \textit{transferred} across related tasks. That is, training a model with a longer and related auxiliary task can lead it to generalize to unseen and longer inputs from some other target task. We demonstrate this length generalization transfer across diverse algorithmic tasks, including arithmetic operations, string transformations, and maze navigation. Our results show that transformer models can inherit generalization capabilities from similar tasks when trained jointly. Moreover, we observe similar transfer effects in pretrained language models, suggesting that pretraining equips models with reusable computational scaffolding that facilitates extrapolation in downstream settings. Finally, we provide initial mechanistic evidence that length generalization transfer correlates with the re-use of the same attention heads between the tasks. Together, our findings deepen our understanding of how transformers generalize to out-of-distribution inputs and highlight the compositional reuse of inductive structure across tasks.

papers.title: Towards Inference-time Category-wise Safety Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we steer LLM generations to safety using gradient-free, inference-time steering methods? The paper explores category-specific steering vectors and sophisticated extraction methods for safety steering.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a category-specific inference-time safety steering method for LLMs that uses steering vectors computed from harmful and harmless activations, with unsupervised and guided extraction methods and pruning to improve steering performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates effective category-specific inference-time safety steering for LLMs using activation-based steering vectors, providing best practices and highlighting trade-offs between safety and text quality.
papers.key_findings:
Category-specific steering reduces unsafe responses, with varying effectiveness across harm categories and models.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves safety steering and can retain or improve text quality.
Using generic harmless data (e.g., Alpaca Instructions) for steering vectors can be effective, reducing the need for category-specific harmless data.
Guided activations (filtered by an external safety classifier) can further reduce unsafe responses but may degrade text quality.
The method works better for Llama3-8B than Llama2-7B, and there is a trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.limitation:
Only attention activations were used for steering; other activation types (MLP, residual stream, block outputs) were not explored.
A simple pruning method based on L2 norms was used; more sophisticated pruning could be explored.
The method does not optimize for text quality, leading to potential degradation in helpfulness and coherence.
future_direction: Explore other types of activations or combinations for steering.
Develop better pruning methods to obtain cleaner steering signals.
Add constraints to the steered generation to improve the trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have seen unprecedented advancements in capabilities and applications across a variety of use-cases, safety alignment of these models is still an area of active research. The fragile nature of LLMs, even models that have undergone extensive alignment and safety training regimes, warrants additional safety steering steps via training-free, inference-time methods. While recent work in the area of mechanistic interpretability has investigated how activations in latent representation spaces may encode concepts, and thereafter performed representation engineering to induce such concepts in LLM outputs, the applicability of such for safety is relatively under-explored. Unlike recent inference-time safety steering works, in this paper we explore safety steering of LLM outputs using: (i) category-specific steering vectors, thereby enabling fine-grained control over the steering, and (ii) sophisticated methods for extracting informative steering vectors for more effective safety steering while retaining quality of the generated text. We demonstrate our exploration on multiple LLMs and datasets, and showcase the effectiveness of the proposed steering method, along with a discussion on the implications and best practices.

papers.title: TOAST: Transfer Learning via Attention Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve transfer learning by refocusing model attention on task-relevant features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TOAST, a transfer learning method that freezes the pre-trained backbone and tunes a top-down attention module to steer attention to task-relevant features, achieving state-of-the-art performance with few tunable parameters.
papers.conclusion: Refocusing attention is key to transfer learning; TOAST achieves state-of-the-art results on fine-grained visual classification and instruction-following language generation by steering attention to task-specific features with few tunable parameters.
papers.key_findings:
TOAST outperforms fully fine-tuning, LoRA, and VPT on fine-grained visual classification, e.g., improving average accuracy on FGVC by 5%.
TOAST achieves state-of-the-art on VTAB-1k benchmark, outperforming baselines on 11 out of 18 tasks for ImageNet-1k pre-trained model.
TOAST improves instruction-following language generation, outperforming fully fine-tuned Alpaca and Vicuna models.
TOAST is adaptable to different model architectures (Transformer and ConvNeXt) and tasks (classification, segmentation).
TOAST-Lite, a parameter-efficient version, performs on par with TOAST while tuning fewer parameters.
papers.limitation: Computation overhead due to running the feedforward path twice, approximately doubling FLOPS.
papers.abstract: Transfer learning involves adapting a pre-trained model to novel downstream tasks. However, we observe that current transfer learning methods often fail to focus on task-relevant features. In this work, we explore refocusing model attention for transfer learning. We introduce Top-Down Attention Steering (TOAST), a novel transfer learning algorithm that keeps the pre-trained backbone frozen, selects task-relevant features in the output, and feeds those features back to the model to steer the attention to the task-specific features. By refocusing the attention only, TOAST achieves state-of-the-art results on a number of transfer learning benchmarks, while having a small number of tunable parameters. Compared to fully fine-tuning, LoRA, and prompt tuning, TOAST substantially improves performance across a range of fine-grained visual classification datasets (e.g., 81.1% -> 86.2% on FGVC). TOAST also outperforms the fully fine-tuned Alpaca and Vicuna models on instruction-following language generation. Code is available at https://github.com/bfshi/TOAST.

papers.title: Enhancing Instruction-Following Capabilities in Seq2Seq Models: DoLA Adaptations for T5
papers.research_question: How do instruction-following signals evolve in encoder-decoder models, and why do contrastive decoding methods like DoLa exhibit mixed behavior in T5 architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes layer-wise representational dynamics in FLAN-T5 decoders, finding intermediate layers are volatile, and introduces a gradient-based activation steering method that dramatically improves instruction-following performance on conflicting tasks.
papers.conclusion: Mid-decoder layers are a key locus for controlling instruction-following in T5 models, and activation steering offers a promising alternative to contrastive decoding for improving faithfulness in Seq2Seq architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate decoder layers in FLAN-T5 undergo substantial representational shifts driven by cross-attention, making their projected token distributions unstable.
DoLa's effectiveness on T5 is task-dependent, succeeding when the instruction signal strengthens in later layers but failing when it is weak or overshadowed by natural-language priors.
A gradient-based activation steering method, which injects an 'instruction-compliance' direction into mid-decoder layers, improves MemoTrap performance from 52% to 99.7% for FLAN-T5-Large.
Steering is most effective in a narrow mid-depth region of the decoder, where representations are informative but not yet committed, and less effective in early or final layers.
The work demonstrates that mechanistic, representation-level interventions offer a promising alternative to layerwise contrast in Seq2Seq models.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on the FLAN-T5 family and tasks with clear contrastive supervision at the token level (MemoTrap), which covers only a narrow subset of instruction-following behavior.
The steering directions extracted are specific to the MemoTrap task, with unknown generalization performance across other instruction types.
Experiments center on single-token interventions; steering multi-token or sequence-level constraints may require different formulations.
Diagnostics rely on LM-head projections, which provide a useful but incomplete view of the hidden-state geometry in Seq2Seq models.
future_direction: Developing steering vectors that encode more general behaviors (e.g., following structural constraints or suppressing memorized continuations) rather than being tied to specific token contrasts.
Investigating encoder-side interventions to clarify how instruction information is formed and propagated before decoding begins.
Designing automated, metric-driven procedures for selecting steering layers or identifying coherent gradient directions, reducing the need for manual search.
Evaluating steering across a wider set of instruction types, such as multi-step reasoning, rewriting, and transformation tasks.
Combining activation steering with decoding-time algorithms to create hybrid methods.
papers.abstract: Encoder-decoder models such as FLAN-T5 are finetuned to follow instructions, but often fail when the instructions conflict with memorized continuations ingrained during training. To understand this behavior, we adapt DoLa to FLAN-T5 and examine how representations evolve in the decoder. Our findings show that T5's intermediate layers undergo rapid shifts driven by cross-attention to the encoder. When projected through the language modeling head, each depth presents highly volatile token preferences, leading to unreliable behavior with contrastive decoding. Motivated by this, we introduce a gradient-based activation-steering method that injects an "instruction-compliance" direction into mid-decoder layers, where the representation is both meaningful and still malleable. This intervention dramatically improves MemoTrap performance (52% to 99.7%), demonstrating that mechanistic steering can succeed where contrastive decoding fails in Seq2Seq architectures.

papers.title: Mind the Performance Gap: Capability-Behavior Trade-offs in Feature Steering
papers.research_question: What is the trade-off between behavioral control and task performance when using feature steering methods? Specifically, can feature steering modify target behaviors without degrading model performance on factual reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Feature steering methods (specifically Goodfire's Auto Steer) substantially degrade model performance (accuracy and coherence) even when successfully controlling target behaviors, revealing a critical capability-behavior trade-off. Simple prompting achieves a better balance between behavioral control and performance preservation.
papers.conclusion: Current feature steering methods face a fundamental capability-behavior trade-off that limits their practical deployment in scenarios where task performance cannot be sacrificed. More work is needed to determine if these trade-offs are fundamental or implementation-specific.
papers.key_findings:
Auto Steer successfully increases behavioral control but causes severe degradation in accuracy (from 66% to 46% on Llama-8B and 87% to 73% on Llama-70B) and coherence (from 4.62 to 2.24 on Llama-8B and 4.94 to 3.89 on Llama-70B).
Simple prompting maintains baseline accuracy and coherence levels while achieving modest behavioral improvements, representing the best overall balance.
The combined approach (Auto Steer + prompting) achieves the strongest behavioral modifications on Llama-8B but inherits the coherence degradation and fails to rescue accuracy.
Steering effectiveness and degradation vary by query: emotional and creative behaviors show strong steering effects but catastrophic performance costs, while behaviors naturally elicited by MMLU (e.g., professional, analytical) show minimal additional modification and less degradation.
There is a consistent positive correlation between coherence and accuracy across both model scales (r=0.302 for Llama-8B, r=0.307 for Llama-70B), indicating that coherence degradation directly predicts reasoning capability loss.
papers.limitation:
Only a single feature steering method (Goodfire's Auto Steer) is evaluated, limiting generalizability to other steering techniques.
Only a single steering strength level is tested, which may not capture the full trade-off curve.
Evaluation is limited to the MMLU benchmark, which focuses on factual recall and analytical reasoning, and may not generalize to other task types.
Reliance on LLM-as-judge methodology for coherence and behavior evaluation may introduce biases.
Only Llama model families (8B and 70B) are tested, so findings may not generalize to other architectures.
future_direction: Systematic comparisons across multiple steering methods to determine if trade-offs are fundamental or implementation-specific.
Varying steering strength to characterize the full trade-off curve between behavioral control, coherence, and task performance.
Evaluating steering methods on diverse tasks including open-ended generation, creative writing, dialogue, and code generation.
Validating automated metrics against human evaluation to ensure reliability.
Testing across different model families to establish generality of findings.
papers.abstract: Feature steering has emerged as a promising approach for controlling LLM behavior through direct manipulation of internal representations, offering advantages over prompt engineering. However, its practical effectiveness in real-world applications remains poorly understood, particularly regarding potential trade-offs with output quality. We show that feature steering methods substantially degrade model performance even when successfully controlling target behaviors, a critical trade-off. Specifically, we evaluate Goodfire's Auto Steer against prompt engineering baselines across 14 steering queries (covering innocuous and safety-relevant behaviors) on 171 Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) questions using Llama-8B and Llama-70B, measuring accuracy, coherence, and behavioral control. Our findings show that Auto Steer successfully modifies target behaviors (achieving scores of 3.33 vs. 2.98 for prompting on Llama-8B and 3.57 vs. 3.10 on Llama-70B), but causes dramatic performance degradation: accuracy on the MMLU questions drops from 66% to 46% on Llama-8B and 87% to 73% on Llama-70B, with coherence falling from 4.62 to 2.24 and 4.94 to 3.89 respectively. Simple prompting achieves the best overall balance. These findings highlight limitations of current feature steering methods for practical deployment where task performance cannot be sacrificed. More broadly, our work demonstrates that mechanistic control methods face fundamental capability-behavior trade-offs that must be empirically characterized before deployment.

papers.title: Analogical Reasoning and Prefrontal Cortex: Evidence for Separable Retrieval and Integration Mechanisms
papers.abstract: The present study examined the contributions of prefrontal cortex (PFC) subregions to two component processes underlying verbal analogical reasoning: semantic retrieval and integration. Event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging data were acquired while subjects performed propositional analogy and semantic decision tasks. On each trial, subjects viewed a pair of words (pair 1), followed by an instructional cue and a second word pair (pair 2). On analogy trials, subjects evaluated whether pair 2 was semantically analogous to pair 1. On semantic trials, subjects indicated whether the pair 2 words were semantically related to each other. Thus, analogy--but not semantic--trials required integration across multiple retrieved relations. To identify regions involved in semantic retrieval, we manipulated the associative strength of pair 1 words in both tasks. Anterior left inferior PFC (aLIPC) was modulated by associative strength, consistent with a role in controlled semantic retrieval. Left frontopolar cortex was insensitive to associative strength, but was more sensitive to integration demands than was aLIPC, consistent with a role in integrating the products of semantic retrieval to evaluate whether distinct representations are analogous. Right dorsolateral PFC exhibited a profile consistent with a role in response selection rather than retrieval or integration. These findings indicate that verbal analogical reasoning depends on multiple, PFC-mediated computations.

papers.title: Executive control in analogical reasoning: Beyond interference resolution
papers.abstract: In recent studies, analogy-making has been shown to depend on the ability to resist interference.
